questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: A fresh Next.js scaffold has a Next.js-logo demo page, and an also nearly-empty next.config.ts. What's the right move for each on day one?

options.label: Delete the demo content; keep next.config.ts even though it looks nearly empty — it's load-bearing plumbing
Delete both — an empty-looking config file is safe to remove and rebuild later
Keep both — the demo content is useful reference for how routing works

questions.explanation: The demo content is disposable; the config file only looks empty because its defaults haven't needed changing yet — it's already doing its job.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: What's the actual signal that a chunk of JSX is worth extracting into its own component?

options.label: It has an identity independent of what's around it — you could describe it in a sentence that isn't 'the rest of the page'
The containing file has crossed roughly 150 lines
It's been copy-pasted at least once already

questions.explanation: Length is a lagging symptom, not the test. A `PageContent` component that's just the whole tangle relocated to a new file fails this test even though it did shrink the original file.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: Two sibling components three lines apart in the same file both need the same array of briefs. What's the right fix, and when would Context actually be the right call instead?

options.label: Lift the state to their nearby common ancestor and pass it as props; reach for Context only when there's no useful nearby common ancestor at all
Always use Context for anything shared by more than one component
Each component should keep fetching and storing its own copy — that's simpler than coordinating

questions.explanation: This is the WeeklyCount bug from the module: two copies of the same fact with nothing keeping them in sync. Lifting state to a nearby ancestor fixes it without needing Context's machinery at all.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: What's the deciding question for whether a screen should get its own route versus staying a conditional view on the same page?

options.label: Would a user plausibly want to bookmark, share, or navigate directly to that exact state?
Is the screen visually different enough from the current one?
Does the screen take more than one API call to render?

questions.explanation: A brief's detail view passes this test — someone should be able to send a client a direct link. A sort-order toggle fails it; nobody bookmarks a specific sort order.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Where should an AI call be placed relative to a CLI tool's fast, frequently-run default path?

options.label: Behind an explicit flag or subcommand a user reaches for on purpose, kept off the fast default path
On the default path, so users get the benefit automatically without needing to know a flag exists
It doesn't matter as long as the call eventually completes

questions.explanation: A fast, constant command has no room in its latency budget for a network call; a slow, occasional one might. The decision is per-command, based on that command's existing frequency and speed.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Why does caching an AI response by a hash of the input and the prompt version work better than manual cache invalidation?

options.label: A real change to either one naturally produces a different hash, invalidating the cache automatically instead of requiring someone to remember to clear it
Hashing makes the cache lookup faster than a plain key would
It isn't actually better — manual invalidation is more reliable

questions.explanation: The hash-based key means a stale cache entry is structurally impossible for a changed input or prompt — there's nothing to remember to invalidate.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: A batch AI operation is about to process hundreds of items at real cost. What pattern does this deserve, per the module on keeping cost predictable?

options.label: A confirm-by-default, --yes-to-bypass prompt showing the estimated cost before it's spent — same pattern as any other consequential action
No special handling — the API's own rate limits will catch anything excessive
A hard cap that silently truncates the batch once a cost threshold is hit

questions.explanation: The module treats a large predictable spend the same as any other destructive or consequential action: show the cost, confirm by default, let --yes skip it deliberately.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: Why does a raw stack trace fail as an error message, even though it technically contains the information about what went wrong?

options.label: It doesn't state what happened, why, or what to do next in language the person reading it can act on
Stack traces are always factually wrong about the actual cause
Nothing is wrong with a stack trace as the default error view

questions.explanation: A good error message answers what happened, why, and what to do next — a stack trace answers none of those for the person actually reading it, even when it's technically accurate.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: A batch job catches every error internally so it never crashes. Why might it still be wrong to exit 0 at the end?

options.label: Surviving a failure and succeeding are different claims — if anything in the batch actually failed, the exit code needs to say so
It's not wrong — catching every error and exiting 0 is always the correct behavior for a batch job
Exit codes only matter for interactive commands, not batch jobs

questions.explanation: A caller checking the exit code needs to know whether the batch actually succeeded, not just that the process didn't crash — those are different facts.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: Why does a unit test of an internal function fail to exercise the same things a real CLI invocation does?

options.label: It never touches argument parsing, exit codes, or stdout/stderr routing — the exact three things a script calling the CLI actually depends on
Unit tests are strictly worse than integration tests in every situation
It's not actually different — a unit test covers everything a real invocation does

questions.explanation: Testing a CLI by spawning the real binary and asserting on stdout, stderr, and exit code separately is the only way to exercise the argument-parsing and exit-code wiring a plain unit test skips entirely.

title: Why the API key can never reach the browser
description: Understanding exactly how an API key leaks from client-side code even when it isn't printed to the console, and what a route handler buys that direct client-side calls can't.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the specific mechanism by which a client-side API key becomes visible to any visitor
Distinguish what a server-side route handler protects from what an environment variable alone protects

contentSections.title: The key that was never logged and still leaked

contentSections.body: briefdesk's first proof-of-concept calls Claude directly from a client component, using `NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. The developer is careful — nothing is `console.log`'d, the key never appears in a commit, there's no obvious leak in the code review. Three days after a soft launch, the Anthropic usage dashboard shows four times the expected spend.

contentSections.scenario: The key is stored in an environment variable prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_`, which Next.js is documented to inline into the client-side JavaScript bundle at build time — by design, for values genuinely meant to be public, like an analytics ID.
contentSections.question: Given nobody logged the key anywhere, how did it end up exposed?

options.label: The GitHub repository containing the code must have been compromised
The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix causes Next.js to inline the value directly into the JavaScript bundle every browser downloads — anyone can read it from the built files, no logging required
Someone on the same network as a user intercepted the request and read the key from network traffic

feedback.compromised-repo: No breach is needed — the key was never a secret in the deployed app to begin with. NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are meant to be embedded in client code by design; the mistake was using that mechanism for something that needed to stay private.
feedback.public-prefix-bundled: Right. NEXT_PUBLIC_ is Next.js's explicit, documented signal that a value should be inlined into the JavaScript every browser downloads — it exists for genuinely public values like an analytics tracking ID. Using it for a secret means the secret is sitting in plain text in the built bundle, readable by opening browser devtools and searching the source, no logging or breach required.
feedback.network-sniffing: HTTPS already protects data in transit between the browser and Anthropic's API — that's not where this leak happened. The key was visible before any request was even sent, sitting in the static JavaScript file the browser downloaded to load the page at all.

contentSections.mechanism: **A `NEXT_PUBLIC_`-prefixed (or any client-bundled) environment variable isn't hidden by not being logged — it's compiled directly into the JavaScript source every visitor's browser downloads, and reading it requires nothing more than opening devtools' Sources tab.** The mistake wasn't a leak in the traditional sense; it was using the public-value mechanism for a value that was never supposed to be public.

contentSections.body: A NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed key isn't leaked by a mistake in logging — it's compiled straight into the browser bundle by design. The fix is a plain env var read only by server-side code the browser never receives.

contentSections.title: What the server actually adds, beyond hiding the key

contentSections.body: "We moved the key server-side" sounds like the whole fix. It buys more than that — a route handler is also the only place briefdesk can validate what's being sent to Claude, cap how much a single request can cost, or stop a request before it happens at all. None of that is possible when the browser talks to Claude directly.

contentSections.scenario: With the key safely server-side, briefdesk's /api/brief route now sits between the browser and Claude. Consider what that position actually enables.
contentSections.question: Which of these does moving the call server-side genuinely enable, beyond just hiding the API key? Select all that apply.

items.label: Rejecting a request before it reaches Claude if clientNotes is empty or absurdly large
Enforcing a fixed max_tokens ceiling regardless of what a modified client sends
Limiting how many requests a single user can make per minute, something a browser-only setup has no way to enforce
Guaranteeing Claude's output is always factually correct
Making the underlying model itself respond faster

explanation.validate-input: A route handler is a real checkpoint — it can look at the request and simply not call Claude at all if the input is obviously malformed or empty, something impossible to enforce from a browser that talks directly to Anthropic.
explanation.cap-tokens: Because the server constructs the actual API call, it controls max_tokens regardless of what a browser sends — a modified or malicious client can't override a limit it never gets to set in the first place.
explanation.rate-limit: Rate limiting (this module's last lesson) is only possible from a position that sees every request — a browser calling Claude directly has no shared, trustworthy place to count requests across users; the server does.
explanation.guarantee-quality: Nothing about server-side placement changes what the model itself produces — moving the call doesn't touch Claude's actual output quality or correctness, which is a separate concern this module doesn't claim to solve.
explanation.speed-up-model: The route handler adds a network hop, if anything — it doesn't make the model faster. Its value is control and safety, not raw speed.

contentSections.synthesis: Hiding the key is the reason a server-side call is non-negotiable, but it isn't the only thing the server-side position buys — it's also the only place any of this module's later lessons (streaming, retries, rate limiting) are even possible to build.

contentSections.body: This reframes the rest of the module: every lesson from here — streaming a response, handling a timeout, rate limiting an endpoint — depends on the call already living behind a server-side route handler. None of it is retrofittable onto a browser calling Claude directly, because the browser has no trustworthy, shared position to do any of it from. Getting the key off the client isn't just a security fix in isolation; it's the prerequisite that makes everything else in this module buildable at all.

A server-side route handler isn't just where the key hides — it's the only position from which validating input, capping cost, and rate limiting are even possible, which is why every later lesson in this module depends on it.

title: A minimal server route that proxies the call
description: Writing a Route Handler that forwards a request to Claude and returns a clean, frontend-friendly response, without leaking internal API shapes or crashing on a malformed request.

learningObjectives.text: Write a Route Handler that validates input before calling Claude
Shape a proxy route's response so the frontend never depends on Anthropic's raw API shape

contentSections.title: The proxy that just forwards everything

contentSections.body: A first-draft `/api/brief` route takes whatever the browser sends, hands it straight to `client.messages.create(req.body)`, and returns `message` untouched. It works for the happy path. It also means the frontend now has to understand Anthropic's exact response shape — `content[0].text`, `stop_reason`, `usage` — and any change to that shape on Anthropic's side breaks briefdesk's UI with no warning.

contentSections.question: This route works today. What's the actual design problem with forwarding the request body directly into messages.create, and the raw response directly back to the browser?

options.label: Nothing — await is used correctly and the route functions as intended

The frontend now has to know Anthropic's exact request and response shape, and the browser can send arbitrary fields (model, max_tokens, system) straight through to the API with no server-side control
This should be a GET request, not POST, since it's just fetching a response

feedback.no-await: The async/await usage is fine mechanically — the problem isn't a bug in this narrow sense, it's what the route's shape lets happen.
feedback.leaky-passthrough: Right. Passing `body` straight into `messages.create` means the browser controls every field Anthropic's API accepts — including `model` (letting a client request an expensive model) and `max_tokens` (letting a client uncap cost) — with nothing server-side deciding what's actually allowed. And returning `message` unmodified means the frontend has to parse Anthropic's exact response shape, coupling briefdesk's UI to an external API's internal structure that can change independent of briefdesk's own release schedule.
feedback.wrong-http-method: POST is the right choice here — the request has a body (the client notes) and triggers an action with a real cost, which is exactly what POST is for. The method isn't the issue.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a route that defines its own request and response contract, independent of Anthropic's: accept only the specific fields briefdesk actually needs (`clientNotes`), construct the Claude API call itself with `model` and `max_tokens` fixed on the server, and return a shape the frontend defines and controls (`{ brief: string }`), not whatever Anthropic happened to send back.

contentSections.body: A proxy route should define its own request and response shape, validate before calling Claude, and fix model/max_tokens server-side — forwarding the browser's body and Anthropic's response unmodified hands control to the client.

contentSections.title: What the frontend should never see

contentSections.body: Claude returns a rate-limit error. briefdesk's route catches the exception and forwards Anthropic's raw error object straight to the browser — including an internal request ID and a message referencing Anthropic's own account limits. The frontend renders it verbatim: 'anthropic.RateLimitError: Number of request tokens has exceeded...'. A user has no idea what that means or what to do.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's route currently does `catch (err) { return Response.json(err); }` — forwarding whatever Anthropic's SDK throws directly to the browser, unmodified, for every failure type.
contentSections.question: What should the route send the browser instead, and where should the raw error detail go?

options.label: Keep forwarding the raw error — it's the most accurate description of what happened
Log the raw error server-side, and send the browser a plain-language message on a status code it can branch on
Catch the error and return a generic 200 OK with empty content, so the UI never has to handle an error state

feedback.raw-forward: Accurate to Anthropic's internals isn't the same as useful to briefdesk's user — a message built for a developer debugging the Anthropic SDK tells a person writing a client brief nothing about what to do next.
feedback.shape-and-log: Right. The raw error is genuinely useful — just not to the browser. Server-side logs are where a developer debugging the issue should find it; the browser needs a plain-language message and a status code it can act on, the same shaping discipline as a success response.
feedback.swallow-silently: This hides the failure entirely — the user has no idea their brief wasn't generated, and might assume it worked. A silent fake success is worse than a clearly shown error.

contentSections.concept: **Errors need the same shaping discipline as success responses: the raw detail goes to server-side logs where it's useful for debugging, and the browser gets a stable, plain-language message on a status code it can branch on — never the provider's raw exception forwarded as-is.**

contentSections.body: Errors need the same shaping as success responses — log the raw provider error server-side, and return the browser a plain, briefdesk-defined error on a status code the frontend can branch on.

title: Streaming a response into the UI as it arrives
description: Streaming Claude's response through a Route Handler using Server-Sent Events, and reading that stream on the client without waiting for the whole response to land.

learningObjectives.text: Implement a streaming Route Handler that forwards Claude's response chunks as they arrive
Read a streamed response on the client and update the UI progressively

contentSections.title: The 12-second blank screen

contentSections.body: briefdesk's brief-generation call, non-streamed, takes 8 to 14 seconds for a longer set of client notes — Claude reasoning through deliverables, timeline and scope before returning anything. The UI shows nothing for that entire window, then the full brief appears at once. Support gets a message: "is this stuck?"

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to get the same eventual response from Claude: wait for `client.messages.create()` to fully resolve, then send the complete text back in one JSON response — or use `client.messages.stream()` and forward each text chunk to the browser as it's generated, over Server-Sent Events.
contentSections.question: For an 8-to-14-second brief generation, which approach actually changes the total time Claude takes to finish, and which just changes what the user sees while waiting?

options.label: Streaming makes Claude generate the full response faster
Streaming doesn't change total generation time at all — it changes when the user starts seeing output, which is what actually fixes the 'is this stuck?' problem
There's no meaningful difference between the two approaches for a request this length

feedback.streaming-faster: Claude generates tokens at the same underlying rate either way — streaming doesn't change the model's actual throughput. What changes is whether the browser has to wait for every token before seeing any of them.
feedback.streaming-perceived: Right. The 8-to-14-second generation time is unchanged either way — what streaming buys is the first visible words arriving in well under a second, instead of twelve seconds of silence followed by everything at once. That's the entire fix for the 'is this stuck?' report: a user watching text actively appear has no reason to wonder if something's frozen.
feedback.no-difference: The difference is exactly the support complaint — twelve seconds of nothing reads as broken; twelve seconds of visibly arriving text reads as working. Total time is the same; what the user experiences during that time is not.

contentSections.concept: **Streaming doesn't make an AI call faster — it changes a single long silent wait into continuous visible progress, which is what actually reads as "working" instead of "stuck."** The fix for a slow perceived response is very often not making it faster at all — it's making its progress visible.

contentSections.body: Streaming doesn't change how long Claude takes to finish — it changes twelve seconds of silence into twelve seconds of visible progress, which is the entire fix for a response that otherwise reads as frozen.

contentSections.title: Reading the stream on the client

contentSections.body: The route streams correctly — `curl`ing it shows chunks arriving over a couple of seconds. briefdesk's React component still shows nothing until the connection closes, because it's reading the response with `await res.json()`, which by definition waits for the entire body before returning anything.

contentSections.problem: Read a Server-Sent Events stream from /api/brief on the client, appending each chunk of text to a piece of state as it arrives, so the UI updates progressively instead of waiting for res.json().

steps.label: Get a reader from the response body
steps.why: res.body is a ReadableStream — getReader() gives a handle to pull chunks from it manually instead of waiting for the whole thing, which is exactly what res.json() can't do.

steps.label: Loop, reading one chunk at a time
steps.why: Each reader.read() resolves as soon as a chunk arrives from the server — not when the whole stream finishes — which is the mechanism that lets the UI update progressively.

steps.label: Parse each SSE line and update state
steps.why: Each SSE 'data: {...}' line is one small piece of Claude's response — appending it to existing state, rather than replacing state, is what makes the text visibly grow instead of flicker.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a second streaming endpoint, /api/summary, which streams a summary of an already-generated brief back to the client the same way.

blanks.prompt: How do you get a reader capable of pulling chunks from the response body one at a time?
blanks.why: Same mechanism regardless of endpoint — the response body is a ReadableStream, and getReader() is how you consume it incrementally instead of all at once.

blanks.prompt: What condition from reader.read() tells you the stream has ended and you should stop looping?
blanks.why: reader.read() resolves with { done, value } on every call — done becomes true once the server has closed the stream, which is your signal to stop, distinct from any individual chunk's content.

blanks.prompt: Given a decoded chunk of text possibly containing multiple SSE lines, how do you isolate just the actual data payloads?
accept: split on newlines and filter lines starting with 'data: '
blanks.why: A single chunk from the network doesn't necessarily align to exactly one SSE event — splitting and filtering is what correctly separates multiple data: lines that may have arrived together, or handles a data: line split across two chunks if you buffer partial lines.

contentSections.procedure: Reading any SSE stream on the client follows the same shape regardless of what's being streamed: get a reader from res.body, loop reading chunks until done, decode and split each chunk into individual data: lines, and update state incrementally rather than replacing it — the incremental update is what turns a stream of small chunks into text that visibly grows on screen.

contentSections.body: res.json() waits for the entire response body — reading a stream progressively requires res.body.getReader(), a manual read loop, and appending each parsed chunk to state instead of replacing it.

title: Timeouts, retries and a request that never finishes
description: Setting a real timeout on a Claude call so a slow request fails instead of hanging indefinitely, and retrying only the failures where a second attempt has a genuine chance of succeeding.

learningObjectives.text: Set an explicit timeout on a Claude API call rather than relying on a default that may not exist
Distinguish which API failures are worth retrying from which just delay an identical, inevitable failure

contentSections.title: The request nobody told to give up

contentSections.body: A brief generation for an unusually long, rambling client email hangs. Not slow — hung. Ten minutes later it's still "loading" in a user's browser tab, the fetch never resolving either way. Nothing crashed; the request simply never got an answer, and nothing in briefdesk's code ever decided to stop waiting for one.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's /api/brief route calls client.messages.create() with no timeout configured, relying on whatever default the Anthropic SDK and the underlying network stack happen to apply.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure here — is it that the request took an unusually long time, or something else?

options.label: Claude occasionally takes ten-plus minutes to respond to long inputs, and there's nothing to do about that
No explicit timeout was set, so the request had no deadline of its own — a slow or stalled connection could wait indefinitely instead of failing at a bounded, predictable point
This can only be explained by a temporary network outage between briefdesk's server and Anthropic's API

feedback.slow-model: Ten minutes with zero output is well outside Claude's normal response time even for long inputs — this reads as a stalled connection, not ordinary model latency. But even if it were unusually slow generation, the real issue is that nothing in briefdesk's code had decided how long was too long to wait.
feedback.no-explicit-timeout: Right. Without an explicit timeout, a request has no self-imposed deadline — if the underlying connection stalls (a dropped packet, a network hiccup that never fully resolves), the fetch can wait far longer than any reasonable user experience should tolerate, because nothing ever told it 'give up after N seconds.'
feedback.network-outage: An outage is possible but isn't the point — even under a genuine outage, the correct behavior is failing within a bounded time and showing an error, not hanging silently for ten minutes. The missing piece is the timeout itself, regardless of what specifically caused the stall.

contentSections.mechanism: **A request with no explicit timeout has no upper bound on how long it might wait — a stalled connection and a request that's simply taking its time look identical from the outside, and without a deadline, the UI has no way to distinguish 'still working' from 'never coming back.'** The fix isn't detecting the hang after the fact; it's never allowing an unbounded wait in the first place.

contentSections.body: Set an explicit timeout on every Claude call — without one, a stalled request has no deadline of its own and can wait far longer than any real user experience should tolerate.

contentSections.title: The retry that just delays the same failure

contentSections.body: briefdesk adds a retry: any failed Claude call gets tried again automatically, up to three times. A malformed request — a bug that always sends an invalid `messages` array under one specific input shape — now fails the same way three times in a row before finally returning an error, tripling the wait for a failure that was never going to succeed.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's retry logic is about to be built. The candidate failure types it might see from a Claude call: a 429 (rate limited), a 529 (API temporarily overloaded), a 401 (invalid API key), a 400 (malformed request body), and a 403 (account lacks access to the requested model).
contentSections.question: Which of these failure types are worth retrying — where a second identical attempt has a genuine chance of succeeding? Select all that apply.

items.label: 429 — rate limited, too many requests right now
529 — Anthropic's API is temporarily overloaded
401 — the API key is invalid or missing
400 — the request body is malformed (e.g. an empty messages array)
403 — the account lacks access to the requested model

explanation.429: A rate limit is a condition that can genuinely clear between attempts — too much traffic right now doesn't mean too much traffic 500ms later, which is exactly what backoff-and-retry is for.
explanation.529: Temporary overload on Anthropic's side is, by definition, temporary — a short wait and a second attempt has a real chance of landing after the overload passes.
explanation.401: An invalid or missing key is a fact about the request's credentials that a retry does nothing to change — the same key fails the same way every time until someone fixes the key itself.
explanation.400: A malformed request body will be malformed on every identical retry — nothing about resending the exact same bad payload makes it well-formed the second time.
explanation.403: Lacking access to a model is an account-level fact, not a transient condition — retrying the identical request doesn't grant access it didn't have a moment ago.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line is whether the *cause* of the failure is a fact about the request itself (malformed body, wrong credentials, no access) or a transient condition of the system right now (overloaded, rate limited) — only the second category has any real chance of resolving between one attempt and the next.

contentSections.body: Retry only failures where the underlying cause can plausibly be gone on a second try (rate limits, temporary overload) — retrying a malformed request or an invalid key just delays an identical, inevitable failure.

title: Rate limiting your own endpoint before someone else costs you money
description: Adding a rate limit to a Claude-backed endpoint so one user, one bug, or one bot can't run up an unbounded API bill, and choosing a limit that fits the actual usage pattern.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an endpoint calling a metered AI API needs its own rate limit independent of the provider's
Implement a simple per-user rate limit on a Route Handler

contentSections.title: The bug that looked like traffic

contentSections.body: A frontend bug — a `useEffect` with a missing dependency array — causes briefdesk's brief-generation call to re-fire on every keystroke in an unrelated field, for one unlucky user, for about four minutes before anyone notices. Four minutes at several calls per second is thousands of billed Claude requests, for zero real briefs produced.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk has no rate limiting on /api/brief. Anthropic's own account-level rate limits exist and would eventually kick in, but only after a much higher volume than one buggy browser tab produces.
contentSections.question: Why isn't relying on Anthropic's own account-level rate limits enough here? Select all that apply.

items.label: Anthropic's limit is per API key, across briefdesk's entire user base — one misbehaving browser tab can eat a meaningful share of it without coming close to tripping it
Every one of those thousands of accidental calls is billed, whether or not Anthropic's rate limit ever engages — the cost problem exists independent of whether the API ever says no
Anthropic doesn't actually enforce any rate limits, so nothing would stop this at any volume
While the bug runs, it can also degrade briefdesk's real users' experience by consuming a shared budget or triggering the account-level limit for everyone

explanation.per-account-not-per-user: Anthropic's rate limit is a ceiling on the whole account's traffic, not a per-user one — a single buggy tab has to reach that entire account-wide ceiling before Anthropic's own limit does anything, which is a much higher bar than 'this one user is clearly misbehaving.'
explanation.cost-not-just-availability: Rate limiting exists for two separate reasons: staying available (not getting throttled) and controlling cost (not paying for calls nobody needed). Anthropic's limit only addresses the first — every call under that ceiling is still billed in full, bug or not.
explanation.anthropic-limits-dont-exist: Anthropic does enforce real rate limits — the point isn't that they're absent, it's that they're scoped to the whole account and calibrated for legitimate high-volume use, not for catching one misbehaving client quickly.
explanation.affects-other-users: If the buggy tab's volume is large enough to approach Anthropic's account-level ceiling, briefdesk's actual users sharing that same API key could start seeing their own legitimate requests throttled — one bug becomes everyone's problem.

contentSections.synthesis: Anthropic's rate limits protect Anthropic's infrastructure at the account level. Nothing protects briefdesk's own bill, or one user's experience from a bug affecting everyone, except a rate limit briefdesk enforces itself, scoped to what a single legitimate user actually needs.

contentSections.body: Anthropic's own rate limits protect its infrastructure at the whole-account level — they don't stop one buggy tab from running up real cost long before that ceiling is reached. Rate limit your own endpoint, scoped to what one legitimate user actually needs.

contentSections.title: Picking a limit that fits real usage, not a guess

contentSections.body: A teammate sets briefdesk's rate limit to 1 request per minute, "to be safe." A designer working through six client intake calls back-to-back on a real Monday morning hits the limit constantly, waiting a full minute between briefs that used to take seconds to generate.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's actual usage logs show a designer working through a batch of client intake notes typically generates a new brief once every 15-40 seconds — reading the previous one, tweaking notes, regenerating.
contentSections.question: Given that real usage pattern, roughly how many requests per minute should briefdesk's rate limit actually allow to avoid blocking legitimate work, while still catching a runaway bug firing many times per second?
contentSections.explanation: Something in the range of 5-8 per minute comfortably covers the real pattern (a brief every 15-40 seconds is roughly 2-4 per minute at a normal pace, with headroom for a faster burst) while still catching a bug that fires on every keystroke — which would hit even a limit of 6 within a second or two, long before it accumulates real cost. A limit of 1/minute, chosen 'to be safe' without checking real usage, actively breaks the tool for its actual users while barely changing how fast a true runaway bug gets caught.

contentSections.body:
A rate limit chosen without looking at real usage is a guess in both directions — too loose to actually catch a bug quickly, or too tight to let a real user work. The number worth setting is derived from how the tool is genuinely used: look at how often a real session calls the endpoint under normal, non-buggy conditions, then set a ceiling comfortably above that but still tight enough that a bug firing dozens of times a second gets caught within a second or two, not a minute.

This is the same principle CLI tools apply to defaults — the CLI-design module's rule that a default should fit the common case, not an arbitrary safe-sounding number. A rate limit is a default too: it should be shaped by what legitimate use actually looks like, checked against logs or a realistic estimate, not picked as a round number that feels cautious.

Set a rate limit from real usage data, not a cautious-sounding round number — too tight breaks legitimate work, and a limit chosen without checking usage patterns is a guess that might not even catch a bug faster.

title: Fix seven insecure or broken API integrations
description: Seven drills applying the module's filters — key placement, request/response shaping, streaming, timeouts and retries, and rate limiting — to Claude integrations you haven't seen before.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's Claude-integration filters to unfamiliar route handlers at speed
Identify the specific security or reliability mistake in a real integration snippet

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Add a properly-proxied Claude feature to your app
description: Build (or fix) a real Claude-backed feature end to end: key server-side, a shaped request/response contract, a streamed response, and a working rate limit — self-checked against this module's rubric.

learningObjectives.text: Build a server-side proxy route for a Claude feature that never exposes the API key to the client
Add streaming and rate limiting to a working Claude-backed endpoint

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter in this module — key kept server-side, a request/response shape you own, a stream instead of a silent wait, a timeout and a sane retry, a rate limit sized to real usage — is easiest to verify on a real, working feature. This lab builds one Claude-backed feature (in briefdesk or your own app) all the way through, end to end.

contentSections.title: A properly-proxied Claude feature
contentSections.brief: Pick one real feature that calls Claude — briefdesk's brief generation, or an equivalent feature in your own app (a summarizer, a rewriter, a classifier). If a client-side or unsafe version already exists, you're fixing it in place; if not, you're building it from scratch. By the end, the API key never reaches the browser, the response streams, and a rate limit protects the endpoint.
contentSections.deliverable: A working feature with the key server-side, streaming output, and a rate limit

stages.title: Move the call server-side and shape the contract
stages.instructions: Confirm (or build) a Route Handler that holds the Claude call, reading the API key from a non-NEXT_PUBLIC_ environment variable. Validate the request body before calling Claude. Define your own request shape (only the fields the feature actually needs) and your own response shape (not Anthropic's raw message object) for both success and error cases.
stages.checkpoint: The API key exists only in server-side code; the route rejects invalid input before calling Claude; success and error responses use a shape you defined, not Anthropic's raw shapes.

stages.title: Stream the response
stages.instructions: Convert the route to stream Claude's response using Server-Sent Events, and update the client to read the stream progressively (via res.body.getReader()) instead of waiting for the full response with res.json(). Confirm the UI visibly updates as text arrives, not all at once at the end.
stages.checkpoint: Text visibly appears progressively in the UI as Claude generates it, not in one block after the full response completes.

stages.title: Add a timeout, a sane retry, and a rate limit
stages.instructions: Set an explicit timeout on the Claude call. Add a retry only for genuinely retryable failures (429, 529, 5xx) with backoff, not for malformed-request or auth failures. Add a per-user (or per-IP) rate limit sized to a real estimate of how often a legitimate user actually calls this feature, and confirm — by testing it directly — that it actually triggers under rapid repeated calls.
stages.checkpoint: A timeout is set explicitly; retries only fire for retryable failure types; the rate limit has been tested and genuinely blocks rapid repeated calls with a clear error.

rubric.criterion: The API key never reaches the client
rubric.meets: No NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix on the key, and it's read only inside server-side code (a Route Handler, Server Action, or Server Component).

rubric.criterion: The route defines its own request/response contract
rubric.meets: The frontend never depends on Anthropic's raw request or response shape for either success or error cases.

rubric.criterion: The response streams
rubric.meets: Text visibly appears progressively as it's generated, using SSE and a client-side read loop, not a single res.json() wait.

rubric.criterion: Timeouts and retries are deliberate
rubric.meets: An explicit timeout is set; retries are limited to failure types where a second attempt has a real chance of succeeding.

rubric.criterion: A rate limit is tested, not assumed
rubric.meets: The limit was verified by actually triggering it with rapid repeated calls, and its number is justified against a real or realistic usage estimate rather than an arbitrary round number.

contentSections.body: A Claude integration isn't 'done' when the happy path works in a demo — it's done when the key can't leak, the wait is visible, and a bug or a bad actor can't run up an unbounded bill.

Making Claude's underlying model respond faster

title: Hierarchy: what the eye should hit first
description: Giving one element on a screen the clearest visual weight so the eye has somewhere obvious to land, instead of letting every element compete at the same volume.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which element on a screen currently has the strongest visual weight, and whether that's the right element
Apply size, weight, color and spacing to make one action visually dominant on a screen

contentSections.title: Everything bold is nothing bold

contentSections.body: briefdesk's dashboard has a page heading, a "Generate brief" button, a "View history" link, and a status line reading "3 briefs this week" — all rendered at 16px, all the same gray-900, all the same font-weight. A first-time user stares at it for a second longer than they should, because nothing tells their eye where to start.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's dashboard renders four elements at identical visual weight: the page heading ("Dashboard"), the primary action ("Generate brief"), a secondary link ("View history"), and a status line ("3 briefs this week"). All four are 16px, font-weight 400, color #111827.
contentSections.question: Someone lands on this screen wanting to generate a brief, which is the thing they came to do. What's actually wrong with how it's currently styled?

options.label: Nothing is visually louder than anything else, so the eye has no signal for which element matters most right now
There's too much text on the screen — the fix is to remove the status line and the history link entirely
Gray-900 is the wrong color for a dashboard — a lighter gray would look more modern

feedback.no-dominant-element: Right. Equal weight across every element means equal weight across every element — there's no signal telling the eye "start here." The fix isn't removing content, it's making the one action a first-time user actually needs (Generate brief) visually louder than the others, so it's the first thing the eye lands on without having to read every line to figure out what matters.
feedback.too-much-text: The amount of content isn't the problem — a status line and a history link are both legitimately useful on a dashboard. The problem is that all four elements are shouting at the same volume, so nothing stands out as the one to act on first. Removing content doesn't fix a hierarchy problem; it just makes the screen sparser while still flat.
feedback.wrong-color: The exact shade of gray isn't what's causing the confusion — even a different single shared color, applied uniformly to all four elements, would leave them all still equal to each other. The issue is the lack of contrast *between* elements, not the specific color chosen for all of them.

contentSections.concept: **Visual hierarchy means one element is clearly louder than the rest — bigger, bolder, higher-contrast, or better-positioned — so the eye has an obvious first stop.** When every element is styled identically, nothing is actually emphasized, even if every individual choice (the font, the color, the size) was reasonable on its own.

contentSections.body:
Hierarchy is built from a small set of levers, used deliberately rather than uniformly: - **Size** — a 24px heading versus 14px body text tells the eye which one to read first. - **Weight** — `font-semibold` versus `font-normal` separates "this matters" from "supporting detail" even at the same size. - **Color and contrast** — a solid `bg-blue-600` button against a page of grays is louder than any amount of size alone could make it. - **Spacing** — the element with the most breathing room around it reads as more important, independent of its own styling. Applied to briefdesk's dashboard: ```tsx

Dashboard

View history

3 briefs this week

``` The heading is now clearly a heading. The primary button is the only solid-colored, high-contrast element on the screen — it wins the eye by default. The link and the status line both stepped back to `text-sm text-gray-500`, not because they're unimportant, but because *this screen* has exactly one thing it wants a first-time user to do first.
Hierarchy comes from deliberate contrast between elements — one thing bigger, bolder, or higher-contrast than the rest — not from every element being styled at the same, safe, uniform weight.

contentSections.title: The one thing everything else has to lose to

contentSections.body: A teammate reviewing briefdesk's form points out that "Generate brief" and "Cancel" are both solid blue buttons, side by side, same size. Technically both are styled — the problem is they're styled the same, which means the form is telling the user two things are equally worth doing.

contentSections.scenario: A single screen — briefdesk's brief-generation form — has a submit button, a cancel button, a "save as draft" link, and a "delete" icon button in the corner.
contentSections.question: Of those four actions, how many should get the loudest, highest-contrast visual treatment on this screen (the treatment "Generate brief" got in the previous section)?
contentSections.explanation: Exactly one. "Generate brief" is what this screen exists for — it gets the solid color, the size, the position that makes it the obvious first stop. "Cancel" and "save as draft" are real, legitimate actions, but they're secondary: a text link or an outlined button, not a second solid-blue button competing for the same attention. "Delete" is even further down — small, often gray or requiring a second confirming click, because it's destructive and the interface shouldn't make it easy to reach by accident. A screen with two loudest elements has, functionally, zero — the user's eye still doesn't know where to start, just now between two options instead of four.

contentSections.body:
This is the practical rule hierarchy reduces to on any single screen: **decide the one action you want a user to take, style everything else to visibly lose to it, and resist giving a second element the same treatment out of a sense of fairness.** In Tailwind terms, that usually means one `bg-blue-600` (or whatever the primary color is) button per screen, everything else using `border` outlines, plain text links, or muted gray: ```tsx
``` Three buttons, three clearly different weights, one obvious first choice. This isn't about making secondary actions ugly or hard to find — "Save as draft" is still a solid, legible button — it's about making sure only one of them is *shouting*.
A screen with two equally loud elements has, functionally, no hierarchy at all — decide the one primary action and let everything else visibly step back from it.

title: A design system of five decisions, not fifty
description: Fixing a type scale, a color pair, a spacing scale, a border-radius and a shadow once, in one place, instead of every component re-deciding them from scratch.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when styling drift (multiple similar-but-different colors, spacings, radii) is caused by missing shared tokens rather than carelessness
Define a minimal design system — five fixed decisions — that a small app's components can draw from instead of re-deciding

contentSections.title: Every PR invents a new blue

contentSections.body: briefdesk's primary button is `bg-[#3b5fe2]`. The nav link's hover state is `bg-blue-600`. A badge on the pricing page uses `bg-indigo-500`. All three read as "blue" from across the room, and all three are subtly different, because three different people styled three different components on three different days without a shared answer for what "the blue" actually is.

contentSections.question: Each component works fine on its own. What's the actual flaw here, and what would fixing it require touching?

options.label: There's no single shared "primary color" decision — each component picked its own blue independently, so the app's blue drifts slightly by component and there's no one place to change it
Indigo-500 and blue-600 are objectively wrong shades — the fix is picking a single objectively correct blue
The real problem is having three separate components at all — they should be merged into one

feedback.no-shared-token: Right. Nothing here is a wrong shade in isolation — the problem is there's no single decision called "primary color" that all three components reference. Each one made its own independent, reasonable-looking choice, and the result is three slightly different blues across the app with no single place to fix or update them together.
feedback.wrong-shade: There's no objectively correct blue in a vacuum — `#3b5fe2`, `blue-600`, and `indigo-500` are all plausible primary colors on their own. The actual defect isn't the specific shade any one component picked, it's that three components picked independently instead of referencing one shared decision.
feedback.too-many-components: A button, a nav link, and a badge are legitimately different components doing different jobs — merging them wouldn't make sense structurally. The fix isn't fewer components, it's giving the components that exist a shared color decision to pull from instead of each inventing its own.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a single token — one primary color, defined once in `tailwind.config.ts` or a CSS variable — that all three components reference instead of hardcoding their own value. That turns "three components with drifting blues" into "one decision, applied consistently, changeable in one place."

contentSections.body:
A design system, at the smallest useful size, is **five fixed decisions written down once**, not fifty ad hoc choices made component by component:

1. **Type scale** — 3-4 font sizes (e.g. `text-sm`, `text-base`, `text-xl`, `text-2xl`) and nothing between them.
2. **Color pair** — one primary color, one neutral gray scale. Everything else (success, warning, danger) can wait until a real use case needs it.
3. **Spacing scale** — a fixed rhythm (Tailwind's default 4px-based scale: `2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24`) used instead of arbitrary values like `p-[13px]`.
4. **One border-radius** — `rounded-md` everywhere a radius is needed, not `rounded-sm` here and `rounded-lg` there by feel.
5. **One shadow** — a single `shadow-sm` or `shadow-md` for anything elevated (cards, dropdowns, modals), not a new shadow value invented per component.

None of this requires a design tool or a component library — it's five decisions, written down, that every new component checks against before inventing its own answer.
Styling drift — three slightly different blues, four different radii — usually isn't carelessness, it's the absence of one shared decision that every component would otherwise reference.

contentSections.title: Five decisions, written down once

contentSections.body: A new contributor to briefdesk opens a PR adding a settings panel and asks in the PR description: "what blue do I use for the save button, and what radius for the panel corners?" There should be one obvious, findable answer — not a guess based on what looked right in the last component they opened.

contentSections.intro: Turn briefdesk's scattered choices into briefdesk's actual five-decision design system, expressed as Tailwind config tokens a new contributor can look up instead of guessing.

fields.prompt: briefdesk currently has bg-[#3b5fe2], bg-blue-600, and bg-indigo-500 scattered across three components. What should the design system fix as "the" primary color decision?

options.label: Pick one shade (e.g. blue-600), define it once as a `primary` token, and have all three components reference it
Keep all three as valid options — variety keeps the UI visually interesting
Leave the choice to whoever builds each new component, since they know their component best

feedback.one-primary-token: Right — one token, one place to define it, one place to change it later. Every component that needs "the primary color" references the same decision instead of making its own.
feedback.keep-all-three: Three shades of the same color isn't visual interest, it's drift — nothing distinguishes when to use which, so it reads as inconsistency rather than intentional variety.
feedback.per-component-choice: This is exactly the situation that produced three different blues in the first place — leaving it to whoever builds each component is how a design system fails to exist.

fields.prompt: Buttons currently use rounded-md, cards use rounded-lg, and badges use rounded-full. Is that a problem the five-decision system needs to fix?

options.label: Not necessarily — a fully-round badge and a slightly-rounded button/card are a deliberate, small, fixed set of radius choices for different shapes, not drift
Yes — the rule says one radius everywhere, so cards and buttons should also become rounded-full
The safest fix is removing border-radius from everything to avoid the decision entirely

feedback.not-necessarily: Right — "one radius" means one *decided, consistent* choice per shape category, not literally one value everywhere regardless of context. rounded-md for buttons and cards, rounded-full for pill-shaped badges is a fixed, intentional pair of decisions — the drift problem is when the *same kind* of element (three different buttons, say) gets three different radii by accident, not when different element types deliberately look different.
feedback.must-be-one-radius: A rounded-full button and a rounded-full card would look wrong — badges are pill-shaped by design, buttons and cards aren't. The five-decision rule is about eliminating accidental drift within the same category of element, not flattening every category to look identical.
feedback.remove-all-radius: This avoids the decision rather than making it — and a hard-edged UI wasn't the actual goal here. The point of a design system is picking the small set of values deliberately, not avoiding styling choices altogether.

contentSections.body: Write the five decisions down once, in the config, so "what color/radius/spacing do I use" has one findable answer instead of a guess based on whichever component was open last.

title: Loading and empty states as first-class screens
description: Designing what a screen looks like before data exists and while it's arriving, as deliberately as the screen that shows the data — rather than letting both default to a blank flash.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose why a screen flashes blank before content appears, in terms of missing explicit state, not a rendering bug
Design distinct empty-state copy and calls-to-action for genuinely different causes of "nothing to show"

contentSections.title: The screen that flashes before there's anything to show

contentSections.body: briefdesk's list of saved briefs loads by fetching from `/api/briefs` on mount. For about 400ms between the page rendering and the fetch resolving, the screen shows... nothing. No heading, no list, no hint that anything is happening. Then briefs pop in, all at once. Nobody designed that blank half-second — it's just what happens when nothing else was designed for it.

contentSections.scenario: `<BriefList />` fetches on mount and stores the result in `useState<Brief[]>([])`. The component renders `{briefs.map(b => <BriefCard key={b.id} brief={b} />)}` unconditionally — no separate check for whether the fetch has completed yet.
contentSections.question: Why does this produce a blank flash instead of a loading indicator, and what's actually missing?

options.label: The initial state is an empty array, and briefs.map on an empty array renders nothing — which is visually indistinguishable from a genuinely empty list, because the code never distinguishes "still loading" from "loaded and there's nothing here"
React itself is slow to paint the first render, causing the visible delay
The fetch call is just too slow — the real fix is a faster API endpoint

feedback.empty-array-default: Right. `useState<Brief[]>([])` starts as an empty array on purpose — before the fetch resolves, `briefs` genuinely is `[]`, and `[].map()` genuinely renders nothing. The component has no separate concept of "still loading" versus "loaded, and it turns out there's nothing here" — both look identical on screen, because only one state variable exists to represent both situations.
feedback.react-slow: React's own rendering isn't the bottleneck here — mounting and painting an empty list happens near-instantly. The delay is entirely the network round-trip to `/api/briefs`, and the blank screen during that round-trip is a design gap, not a framework performance issue.
feedback.fetch-too-slow: Even a fast fetch (100-400ms is normal for a database read) has a real duration users perceive as a pause — the fix isn't necessarily making it faster, it's designing what the screen shows honestly during that pause, which today is nothing.

contentSections.mechanism: **A component with only one state variable for "the data" can't distinguish "still loading" from "loaded, and empty" — both render as nothing.** The fix isn't a faster fetch, it's an explicit status alongside the data: `'loading' | 'empty' | 'loaded'`, so the component can render something honest for each one.

contentSections.body: A blank flash before content appears usually means "loading" was never given its own explicit state — it's whatever an empty default happened to render, not a screen anyone actually designed.

contentSections.title: An empty list and an empty search result are different screens

contentSections.body: briefdesk's `EmptyBriefsState` says "No briefs yet — generate your first one" with a button. It works fine for a brand-new account. It also shows for a two-year user who just searched their 40 saved briefs for "logo redesign 2019" and got zero matches — where "generate your first one" is nonsense, because they have 39 other briefs sitting right there.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk can show "zero briefs" for at least three different reasons: (1) a brand-new account that has never generated a brief, (2) a search or filter that matched nothing among an account's real briefs, (3) an account that deleted its last remaining brief a moment ago.
contentSections.question: Should all three of these render the same "No briefs yet — generate your first one" empty state?

options.label: No — each cause implies a different next step for the user, so each deserves its own copy and call-to-action, even though the visible list is empty in all three
Yes — the list is empty in all three cases, so one generic empty state covers all of them correctly
Only case 1 needs any copy at all — cases 2 and 3 can just show a blank list, since the user already knows what they did

feedback.no-different-causes: Right. "Generate your first brief" is the correct next step for a brand-new account, actively wrong advice for someone who just filtered 40 real briefs down to zero matches (their next step is "clear the filter," not "start from scratch"), and slightly odd for someone who just deleted their last brief (who might want an undo, not an onboarding pitch). Same visible emptiness, three different correct next steps.
feedback.yes-same-copy: The list being empty is a fact about the UI, not a fact about what the user should do next — and those two things diverge across the three cases. A searcher getting onboarding copy after a failed search reads as the app not noticing what actually happened.
feedback.only-onboarding-needs-copy: A blank list after a search still leaves the user unsure whether the search is broken, whether they mistyped something, or whether there genuinely are no matches — some copy is needed in every case, it's just different copy each time.

contentSections.concept: **"Empty" is a visible state, not a single cause — the right copy and call-to-action depend on why it's empty, not just on the fact that it is.** A true first-time empty state earns onboarding copy; a filtered-to-zero result earns "clear your filters"; neither should borrow the other's message.

contentSections.body: An empty screen has a cause, and the cause — brand-new, filtered-to-zero, just-deleted — determines the right copy and call-to-action; one generic "nothing here" message papers over a real difference.

title: Responsive from a phone in bed, not as an afterthought
description: Building layouts mobile-first with Tailwind's responsive prefixes, and sizing tap targets and control placement for someone using the app one-handed, lying down.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a layout built desktop-first that breaks on small screens, and rewrite it mobile-first with responsive prefixes
Evaluate a screen's tap targets and control placement against one-handed, lying-down use

contentSections.title: Designed at 1440px, tested never below it

contentSections.body: briefdesk's brief detail screen looks great on the designer's laptop: a two-column layout, the brief's notes on the left, deliverables and timeline on the right, both columns comfortably wide. On a phone, the same layout squeezes both columns to about 160px each — every line of text wraps after two or three words, and the whole screen reads like a receipt.

contentSections.question: The layout looks correct on a wide screen. What's the actual flaw, and where does it live in this code?

options.label: `grid-cols-2` applies at every screen width, including phone-sized ones, because it has no responsive prefix scoping it to wider screens
`gap-6` is too large a gap and should be reduced across all screen sizes
Using <section> instead of <div> is the actual cause of the squeeze

feedback.unconditional-two-col: Right. `grid-cols-2` has no breakpoint prefix, so Tailwind applies it at every viewport width — 375px included. The two-column layout is a genuinely good choice on a laptop and a genuinely bad one on a phone, and this class makes no distinction between the two.
feedback.gap-too-large: Even with `gap-6` reduced to `gap-2`, two 160px-wide columns would still wrap every line after two or three words — the gap size is a minor detail next to the fact that there are two columns at all on a screen this narrow.
feedback.wrong-tag: `<section>` is a block-level element with no default width constraints of its own — swapping it for `<div>` would render identically. The squeeze comes entirely from `grid-cols-2` being active at a width where it doesn't fit.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is Tailwind's mobile-first responsive prefixes: unprefixed classes are the default (the smallest screen), and `md:`/`lg:` prefixes override them at wider breakpoints. `className="grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 gap-6 p-4 md:p-8"` stacks the two sections on a phone and switches to two columns only once there's room for them.

contentSections.body:
Tailwind's responsive system is mobile-first: an unprefixed class is the default that applies at *every* width unless a breakpoint prefix overrides it starting at that width. That means the smallest screen should be the one written without any prefix, and wider layouts are additions on top of it — not the other way around: ```tsx

Notes

{brief.notes}

Deliverables

    {brief.deliverables.map(d =>
  • {d}
    • )}
``` `grid-cols-1` is the real default — one column, full width, readable on a 375px phone. `md:grid-cols-2` only takes over at 768px and above, where two columns genuinely fit. Writing it this direction (start narrow, add width-based overrides) means the phone layout was never an afterthought bolted onto a desktop-first grid — it's the baseline everything else builds on.
Write the narrowest layout first, unprefixed, and add md:/lg: overrides for wider screens — a desktop layout with no mobile variant isn't unfinished, it's backwards.

contentSections.title: Touch targets and one-handed thumb reach

contentSections.body: briefdesk's mobile nav has five icon buttons in a row, each about 24px square with 4px of gap between them. A user lying down, thumbing through the app one-handed, taps "Export" and hits "Delete" instead — the two icons are visually distinct but physically too close and too small for a thumb that isn't looking as precisely as a mouse cursor would.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's mobile screen has: (1) five 24px icon buttons in a row with 4px gaps in the bottom nav; (2) a primary "Generate brief" button, 48px tall, centered near the top of the screen; (3) a "Delete brief" icon, 40px, placed directly next to "Export", both easily reachable but visually similar; (4) a settings toggle, 44px tall, placed in the top-right corner of a tall screen.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real problems for someone using the app one-handed, lying down, and worth fixing? Select all that apply.

items.label: The 24px nav icons with 4px gaps (case 1) — below the ~44px minimum comfortable touch target, with too little separation between adjacent targets
The 48px primary button (case 2) — sized correctly, but placed near the top of a tall screen, outside where a thumb comfortably reaches while holding the phone one-handed
"Delete" placed immediately next to "Export" (case 3) — a destructive action sitting right beside a routine one, easy to mis-tap even at 40px
The 44px settings toggle in the top-right (case 4) — correctly sized; being in a corner is fine for an action used rarely, not on the main flow

explanation.small-nav-icons: 24px is well under the roughly 44px most guidance treats as a comfortable minimum touch target, and 4px of gap isn't much margin for a thumb (which covers a wider area than a mouse cursor) to avoid clipping the neighboring icon.
explanation.primary-button-top: Size isn't the issue here — 48px is generous. Position is: on a tall phone held one-handed, the top of the screen is the hardest zone for a thumb to reach without shifting grip, so the single most important action on the screen is placed in the least reachable spot.
explanation.delete-next-to-export: Even at a reasonable 40px, placing a destructive action directly adjacent to a routine one raises the cost of a mis-tap — the fix isn't necessarily resizing, it's separating them or requiring a second confirming step before delete actually happens.
explanation.settings-toggle: This one is fine as designed — 44px meets the target-size guidance, and a corner placement is a reasonable trade-off for an action someone reaches for occasionally, not one that needs to sit in the primary thumb zone.

contentSections.synthesis: Two separate things are being evaluated at once: is the target big enough to hit reliably (size and spacing), and is it *positioned* somewhere a thumb can reach without adjusting grip (bottom and center of the screen beat the top corners, for a one-handed hold). A frequently-used or high-consequence action failing either test is worth fixing; an occasional action in an awkward-but-reachable spot usually isn't.

contentSections.body:
Two practical defaults follow from this: **44px minimum on anything tappable** — `min-h-11 min-w-11` in Tailwind (11 × 4px = 44px) — with real spacing between adjacent targets rather than them touching; and **primary, frequent actions live in the bottom half of the screen**, not the top, because that's the zone a thumb reaches without the hand shifting its grip on the phone: ```tsx // mobile nav — each icon gets a real target, not just a visible one
{navItems.map(item => ( ))}
// primary action, pinned near the thumb zone on mobile, freed up on desktop
``` None of this is about making the app *look* more mobile — it's about the physical reality of a thumb, not a cursor, doing the tapping, often while lying down and not looking as precisely as someone at a desk would.

A tap target needs to be both big enough (roughly 44px, with real spacing from its neighbors) and positioned where a one-handed thumb actually reaches — a correctly-sized button in the top corner of a tall phone screen still fails the second test.

title: Removing a step instead of styling it better
description: Recognizing when the actual friction in a flow is the number of steps, not their visual polish, and deferring everything that isn't required before the very next action.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a flow's friction comes from step count rather than visual styling, and prioritize removal over polish accordingly
Identify which fields in a form genuinely block the next action versus which can be deferred to later

contentSections.title: A prettier five-step form is still five steps

contentSections.body: briefdesk's signup flow has five separate screens: email, password, organization name, a "what do you use briefdesk for" selector, and a confirmation screen. A team spends a sprint polishing every screen's spacing, transitions, and color — each one now looks genuinely great. Signup completion rate doesn't move.

contentSections.scenario: Signup drop-off happens steadily across all five screens rather than concentrating on one — roughly 15-20% of users leave at each step, even after the visual redesign. Time-on-screen for each step didn't meaningfully change either, before or after the redesign.
contentSections.question: Given that drop-off is spread evenly across all five steps and didn't improve after a purely visual redesign, what does that suggest about where the actual friction lives?

options.label: The friction is the number of steps itself — each additional screen is another point where someone can decide to stop, regardless of how well any individual screen is styled
One specific screen is poorly designed and needs to be identified and fixed
Steady drop-off across every step means nothing about the flow can be improved — some users just won't finish signup

feedback.step-count-itself: Right. Even drop-off across every step, unmoved by better visuals, points at the count of steps as the friction — not the quality of any individual screen. Each screen is a fresh decision point ("do I keep going"), and five decision points produce more total drop-off than one, no matter how well each one is designed.
feedback.one-bad-screen: If one screen were uniquely bad, drop-off would spike there specifically — a step with unusually high abandonment relative to its neighbors. Even, steady drop-off across all five is the opposite signature: it points at something true of the flow as a whole (its length), not one weak link in it.
feedback.not-fixable: Nothing about the data rules out improvement — it rules out *visual* improvement as the lever that matters here. The intervention the data actually points toward is reducing the number of steps, which the team hasn't tried yet.

contentSections.mechanism: **Drop-off spread evenly across every step, unmoved by better styling, is the signature of the step count itself being the friction — not any individual screen's quality.** The fix the data points to is combining or removing steps, not a better visual pass on the same five screens.

contentSections.body:
This is worth naming explicitly because it cuts against instinct: when a flow feels clunky, the reflexive fix is to make it look nicer — better spacing, a smoother transition between steps, a cleaner input style. Sometimes that's the right fix. But when the actual complaint is "this takes forever" or "I gave up partway through," polish addresses how each step *feels*, not how many of them there are, and a five-step flow that feels five separate points of friction, no matter how well each individual step is executed.

The ordering worth defaulting to: **ask whether a step can be removed or merged before spending time making it look better.** A signup flow that goes from five screens to two is a bigger improvement to completion rate than five screens each redesigned to perfection — and it's often less total work.
When drop-off is spread evenly across a flow's steps, the fix the data points to is fewer steps — visual polish improves how a step feels, not how many of them stand between someone and finishing.

contentSections.title: Which steps are actually load-bearing

contentSections.body: Cutting briefdesk's signup from five screens to two means deciding which fields are actually required before someone can do anything, and which ones just felt natural to ask for up front because that's how signup forms usually look.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's five signup fields: (1) email address, (2) password, (3) organization name, (4) a "what do you use briefdesk for" multi-select (marketing, agency work, internal tools, other), (5) an email confirmation click.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely have to happen before a new user can reach their first real action (generating a brief)? Select all that apply.

items.label: Email address — needed to create the account and identify the user at all
Password — needed to secure the account before any data is created under it
Organization name — useful for later personalization, but nothing about generating a first brief requires it to exist yet
"What do you use briefdesk for" — valuable for the product team's segmentation, not a blocker for the user's first action
Email confirmation click — protects against fake signups, but doesn't need to happen synchronously before letting the user try the product

explanation.email: This is the account identifier — there's no way to create an account at all without it, so it genuinely blocks everything downstream.
explanation.password: Same category as email — the account can't exist in a usable, secured state without it before anything is stored under that account.
explanation.org-name: This is real, useful data, just not data that blocks the user's very next action. It can be asked for later — in a profile screen, or the first time it's actually needed (say, inviting a teammate) — instead of before they've seen any value from the product.
explanation.use-case-selector: This is the clearest case of data collected for the business's benefit (segmentation, marketing) rather than the user's — it can be asked after signup, or even opportunistically later, without costing the user a completed action first.
explanation.email-confirmation: Confirming an email address matters for account security and deliverability, but it doesn't have to gate the user's first real action — the confirmation can happen in the background (an email sent, a banner shown) while the user is already generating their first brief.

contentSections.synthesis: Two fields are genuinely load-bearing (email, password) — nothing works without them. The other three are real, useful data that briefdesk should still collect, just not as a precondition for a user's first taste of the product. The rule: **ask only what blocks the very next action; defer everything else to a moment after the user has gotten value, or to a background process that doesn't block them at all.**

contentSections.body:
Applied, briefdesk's signup goes from five screens to two:

```tsx
// Screen 1 (the only screen before first use): email + password
<form onSubmit={handleSignup}>
  <input type="email" placeholder="Email" required />
  <input type="password" placeholder="Password" required />
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
// → redirects straight into the app, first brief generation available immediately
```

Organization name gets asked the first time it's actually needed (inviting a teammate, or a one-time prompt on the dashboard the user can dismiss). The use-case selector becomes a single optional question dropped into the dashboard after the first brief is generated — collected, but never blocking. Email confirmation sends in the background and shows a small banner ("check your inbox") without gating anything. This is progressive disclosure: collect what's required now, and ask for the rest exactly when it's needed — or never force it at all.

Ask only what genuinely blocks the user's next action; defer everything else — organization details, segmentation questions, confirmations — to the moment it's actually needed, or push it to the background entirely.

title: Redesign seven cluttered screens
description: Seven drills applying the module's filters — hierarchy, shared tokens, first-class empty/loading states, mobile-first layout, and step removal — to screens you haven't seen before.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's UX filters to unfamiliar screens at speed
Identify the specific styling or flow mistake in a real screen, not just that it feels cluttered

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Redesign one real screen of your app
description: Take one real screen from a working app, audit its hierarchy and states against this module's filters, apply a fix, and document the before-and-after with the specific decisions that changed.

learningObjectives.text: Audit a real screen's hierarchy, tokens, states, responsiveness and step count against this module's filters
Redesign a real screen and document each specific decision that changed and why

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter in this module — one dominant action per screen, five fixed tokens instead of fifty guesses, loading and empty states designed on purpose, mobile-first layout, fewer steps before more polish — is easiest to prove on a real screen you actually maintain. This lab picks one screen from a working app of yours (briefdesk-shaped or otherwise) and redesigns it against a rubric you can check yourself before calling it done.
