contentSections.title: Redesign one screen, and show your work
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, currently-live screen from an app you maintain — a dashboard, a form, a list view, whatever exists. You're not redesigning the whole app. You're auditing this one screen against this module's filters, applying the fixes that actually apply, and producing a before-and-after that names the specific decisions that changed, not just "it looks better now."
contentSections.deliverable: Before-and-after screens with the specific decisions that changed

stages.title: Audit the screen
stages.instructions: Screenshot or sketch the screen as it exists today. For each of this module's five filters, write one honest sentence: is there a clear single dominant action, or several competing? Are colors/spacing/radius/shadow drawn from a fixed set, or improvised per element? Are loading and empty states designed, or do they default to blank/nothing? Does the layout hold up at phone width? Is there a step here that could be removed rather than styled better?
stages.checkpoint: A written audit exists with one honest sentence per filter, naming what's actually wrong (or confirming a filter already passes).

stages.title: Apply the fixes
stages.instructions: Fix whichever filters the audit flagged. This won't be all five for most real screens — pick the two or three that matter most for this specific screen and do them properly rather than touching all five shallowly. Common real fixes: demote every button but one, replace ad hoc colors/spacing with your app's five tokens (or define them now if they don't exist yet), add an explicit loading/empty branch where one was missing, add a mobile-first responsive pass, or cut a step that isn't load-bearing.
stages.checkpoint: The screen is visibly changed in at least two of the five filter areas, and you can name the specific class, state, or field that changed for each.

stages.title: Document the before-and-after
stages.instructions: Put the before and after side by side (screenshots, or before/after code snippets if that's clearer). For each change, write one sentence naming the specific decision — not "improved the hierarchy" but "made 'Generate brief' the only solid-colored button on the screen; 'Save as draft' and 'Cancel' now use an outline and a text link."
stages.checkpoint: A before-and-after exists where every claimed improvement is tied to a specific, nameable decision, not a vague description.

rubric.criterion: The screen has one clear dominant action
rubric.meets: Exactly one element is visually loudest, and it's the action the screen actually exists for — not two competing solid buttons, not zero.

rubric.criterion: Styling draws from a small, named set of decisions
rubric.meets: Colors, spacing, radius, and shadow used on this screen trace back to a fixed token, not an improvised one-off value — and if the tokens didn't exist before this lab, they're written down now.

rubric.criterion: Loading and empty states (if this screen has any async data) are explicitly designed
rubric.meets: There's a real branch for 'still loading' and, if relevant, distinct copy for at least one specific empty-state cause — not a blank default.

rubric.criterion: The layout holds up at phone width
rubric.meets: Checked at a genuinely narrow viewport (not just resized 10% from desktop) — text doesn't wrap after two words, tap targets are reasonably sized and spaced.

rubric.criterion: Every claimed improvement is a specific, nameable decision
rubric.meets: The before-and-after doesn't contain a change described only as 'better' or 'cleaner' — each one names the actual class, state, or field that changed.

contentSections.body: The real test of a redesign isn't whether it looks nicer in a screenshot — it's whether you can name the specific decision behind every change, the same discipline this module asked of the exercises.

title: Checkpoint — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Integrating the Claude API Properly, two from Structuring a Web App That Grows. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User

questions.from: This module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A form has three buttons — submit, save-as-draft, cancel — all styled as identical solid-blue buttons. What's the actual problem, and what's the fix?

options.label: Nothing is visually dominant, so the eye has no signal for the primary action — keep one solid, demote the other two to outline/text
The buttons should all be a different color, not blue, since blue is overused
Nothing is wrong — consistent styling across buttons is good practice

questions.explanation: Three equally loud buttons leave the eye with no obvious first stop. The fix keeps the solid, high-contrast treatment for the one primary action and lets the others visibly step back.

questions.from: This module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: Three components use bg-[#3b5fe2], bg-blue-600, and bg-indigo-500 respectively for what's meant to be "the primary color." What's the underlying issue?

options.label: There's no single shared color token — each component picked independently instead of referencing one fixed decision
One of the three shades is objectively the correct blue and the other two are wrong
This isn't a real problem since all three read as blue from a distance

questions.explanation: None of the three shades is wrong in isolation — the defect is the absence of one shared token that all three components would otherwise reference, which is what a five-decision design system fixes.

questions.from: This module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A list component renders `items.map(...)` directly off a useState that starts as `[]`, with no other status tracked. What does the screen show before the fetch resolves, and why?

options.label: Nothing — an empty array and a not-yet-loaded state render identically, because there's only one state variable representing both
A default browser spinner, automatically
A React error, since items is empty on first render

questions.explanation: The initial empty array is visually indistinguishable from a genuinely empty result — the fix is an explicit loading/empty/loaded status alongside the data, not a faster fetch.

questions.from: This module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A grid is written as `grid-cols-3` with no responsive prefixes. What happens at phone width, and what's the mobile-first fix?

options.label: Three columns render at every width including narrow phones; fix with grid-cols-1 (unprefixed default) and md:/lg: overrides to add columns at wider breakpoints
Tailwind automatically reduces the column count below a certain screen width
Nothing breaks, since grid-cols-3 only applies where three columns physically fit

questions.explanation: Unprefixed classes apply at every width by default — there's no automatic narrow-screen adjustment. Mobile-first means writing the narrowest layout unprefixed and adding wider-screen overrides on top.

questions.from: Previous module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: Why can an Anthropic API key never be sent to the browser, even behind HTTPS?

options.label: Anything shipped to client-side JavaScript is readable by anyone who opens dev tools, regardless of the transport encryption — HTTPS protects data in transit, not code visibility at the destination
HTTPS doesn't encrypt requests originating from the browser, only from servers
It's fine as long as the key is stored in a JavaScript variable instead of a hardcoded string

questions.explanation: HTTPS protects data in transit between client and server — it does nothing to hide code or values that are shipped to and executed in the browser itself, which anyone can inspect via dev tools regardless of how it's stored client-side.

questions.from: Previous module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: What's the point of streaming a Claude response into the UI token by token instead of waiting for the full response and rendering it at once?

options.label: The user sees progress within a second or two instead of staring at a blank state for the full multi-second generation time — perceived latency drops even though total completion time doesn't
Streaming makes the underlying model generate the response faster
It reduces the total number of tokens the API call uses

questions.explanation: Streaming doesn't change the model's generation speed or cost — it changes what the user sees while generation happens, turning a multi-second blank wait into visible, incremental progress.

questions.from: Previous module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: A server route calls Claude with no timeout set. What's the concrete risk, and what's the fix?

options.label: A hung request can tie up server resources indefinitely with no user-facing feedback; the fix is an explicit timeout (e.g. AbortController) with a clear error surfaced to the UI once it fires
There's no real risk — the API always responds within a few seconds
The fix is retrying immediately in a tight loop until a response arrives

questions.explanation: Without an explicit timeout, a stalled request has no defined end state — the fix is an AbortController-based timeout paired with a real error state the UI can show, not an assumption that responses always arrive quickly.

questions.from: Previous module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: Why does an unauthenticated AI endpoint with no rate limit put a real dollar figure at risk, specifically?

options.label: Every request that reaches the endpoint triggers a metered, paid API call — with no limit, a script or bot can trigger an unbounded number of them at the owner's expense
It's a purely theoretical risk since bots don't target small apps
Rate limiting is only about preventing server crashes, not cost

questions.explanation: Each call to a metered AI API costs real money regardless of who or what triggers it — an endpoint with no cap on request volume has no ceiling on that cost, which is a financial risk distinct from (though related to) server load.

questions.from: Older module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: What's the actual signal that a chunk of JSX is worth extracting into its own component?

options.label: It has an identity independent of what's around it — describable in a sentence that isn't 'the rest of the page'
The containing file has crossed roughly 150 lines
It's been copy-pasted at least once already

questions.explanation: Length is a lagging symptom, not the test — a chunk with real independent identity is worth extracting even in a short file, and a long file that's one coherent story might not need splitting at all.

questions.from: Older module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: Two sibling components a few lines apart in the same file both need the same array of data. What's the right fix, and when does Context actually earn its cost instead?

options.label: Lift the state to their nearby common ancestor and pass it as props; reach for Context only when there's no useful nearby common ancestor at all
Always use Context for anything read by more than one component
Each component should keep its own independent copy — simpler than coordinating

questions.explanation: Nearby siblings under a shared parent are a props problem, not a Context problem — Context earns its machinery specifically when consumers are spread apart with no useful common ancestor to lift state to.

title: Deploying to Vercel end to end
description: Connecting a repo to Vercel and understanding what actually happens between a git push and a live URL, including what the platform costs once real usage starts.

learningObjectives.text: Sequence what happens between a git push and a live production URL on Vercel
State what Vercel's free tier includes and what triggers a real cost

contentSections.title: What actually happens after git push

contentSections.body: briefdesk exists locally, running on `localhost:3000`. Someone connects the GitHub repo to Vercel, clicks "Deploy," and ninety seconds later there's a real URL — `briefdesk-abc123.vercel.app` — that works from any phone, anywhere. Nothing about the app changed. What changed was who's now running it.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order they actually happen after connecting a GitHub repo to Vercel and pushing to the main branch.
steps: Vercel detects the push via a GitHub webhook
Vercel spins up a build container and runs the detected framework's build command (e.g. `next build`)
The build output (static assets, serverless/edge functions) is uploaded to Vercel's infrastructure
Vercel's global CDN and routing layer starts serving the new deployment
The production domain (or a generated *.vercel.app URL) now points at this deployment
contentSections.explanation: The trigger is always the push — Vercel isn't polling, it's told via webhook the moment new code lands on a connected branch. Everything after that is Vercel's job, not the developer's: detect the framework (Next.js, in briefdesk's case), run its standard build command, take the output, and put it behind a domain. Nothing about this sequence requires SSH access to a server, manually running a build, or uploading files by hand — that manual process is exactly what a platform like Vercel replaces.

contentSections.body:
The whole point of a platform deploy is that none of those steps are yours to run by hand. `vercel.json` (optional — Vercel auto-detects most frameworks including Next.js without it) can override the build command or output directory, but for a standard Next.js app the defaults just work:

```bash
# one-time setup, from the project root
npx vercel        # links the local folder to a Vercel project, deploys once
npx vercel --prod # explicitly promotes to the production domain
```

After the initial link, every `git push` to the connected branch (main, by convention) triggers a fresh production build automatically — no `vercel --prod` needed again unless deploying from the CLI directly instead of through git. **What this costs:** Vercel's Hobby tier is free and covers a real app in early use — generous build minutes, 100GB of bandwidth a month, unlimited deployments. It's meant for personal and non-commercial projects; the terms require a Pro plan (starting at $20/month per team member) once the project is used commercially or a team collaborates on it, and Pro also raises the bandwidth and build-minute ceilings for anything getting real traffic.

A Vercel deploy is: push triggers a webhook, Vercel builds using the framework's own build command, the output goes live behind a domain — no manual build or upload step, and free on the Hobby tier until the project is commercial or a team is collaborating on it.

contentSections.title: One push, two different domains

contentSections.body: A teammate opens a pull request adding a new feature to briefdesk. Vercel comments on the PR with a link — a completely different URL from `briefdesk.app`, but a fully working, fully deployed copy of the app with just that PR's changes.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's main branch is connected to the production domain briefdesk.app. A teammate opens a pull request with three commits, pushing twice more after the PR is opened (fixing review comments).
contentSections.question: How many distinct preview deployment URLs does this one PR produce across its lifetime — one per PR, or one per push?
contentSections.explanation: One. A PR gets one stable preview URL that updates in place with every new push to that branch — it's not a new URL per commit, which would make it useless to share or bookmark for review. The URL stays constant; what's live behind it changes as new commits land, right up until the PR merges (at which point that branch's preview deployment stops being relevant) or is closed.

contentSections.body: This is the two-domain model that makes Vercel deploys safe to iterate on: **production** is whatever's on the connected branch (usually `main`) and lives at the real domain; **preview** is every other branch and pull request, each getting its own unique, shareable, fully-functional URL that never touches production. A designer can review a PR's actual rendered UI without anyone merging anything, and a bug in a branch never reaches real users because it's simply never on the production domain in the first place. This distinction — and specifically how environment variables differ between the two — is where the next lesson picks up, because "it works on preview" and "it works in production" are not automatically the same claim.
Production is the connected branch at the real domain; every other branch and PR gets its own preview URL that never touches it — one stable URL per PR, updated in place as new commits land.

title: Environment variables per environment, not one shared set
description: Scoping secrets to Production, Preview and Development independently, and using separate test credentials for non-production environments instead of one shared production key.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a preview-only crash caused by an environment variable scoped to the wrong environment
Decide when a non-production environment needs its own separate credentials rather than reusing production ones

contentSections.title: Works in production, crashes in preview

contentSections.body: briefdesk's production site works fine. A teammate opens a PR, checks the preview URL Vercel posted, and the brief-generation button throws "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not defined." The exact same code is running in both places.

contentSections.question: The code is identical in production and preview. What's actually causing the preview-only crash?

options.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is checked only for the Production environment in Vercel's dashboard, so it's genuinely undefined when the same code runs in a Preview build
There's a bug in the route handler that only manifests under preview's build settings
The Anthropic API is rate-limiting requests coming from preview deployments specifically

feedback.scoped-to-prod-only: Right. Vercel's environment variables are scoped per environment by design — a variable checked only for "Production" genuinely does not exist in a Preview build's `process.env`, even though it's the same code, same repo, same commit history. `process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is `undefined` in preview, and the Anthropic client throws exactly the error being seen.
feedback.code-bug: The route handler is identical between environments — there's no preview-specific code path here at all. If it were a code bug, it would fail identically in both places, not selectively in one.
feedback.rate-limit: A rate-limit error from Anthropic's API would look like a 429 response with a rate-limit message, not "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not defined" — this specific error is a client construction failure, happening before any request to Anthropic is even made.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is checking the "Preview" (and usually "Development") boxes alongside "Production" when adding the variable in Vercel's dashboard — or using different values per environment entirely, which is exactly the situation the next section covers.

contentSections.body:
Vercel's environment variables aren't one global bag of key-value pairs — every variable is scoped to one or more of three environments (Production, Preview, Development) independently, checked as separate boxes when it's added:

```
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_TEST    sk-ant-test-...   [ ] Production  [x] Preview  [x] Development
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY         sk-ant-live-...   [x] Production  [ ] Preview  [ ] Development
```

Locally, `.env.local` (gitignored by default in a Next.js scaffold — never commit it) fills the same role as Development-scoped variables in Vercel's dashboard. A variable that's genuinely needed everywhere — say, a public analytics ID — gets all three boxes checked; one that should behave differently per environment (the API key case above) gets different values under different names, or the same name with environment-specific values, scoped deliberately rather than assumed universal. Forgetting to check Preview isn't a rare mistake — it's the default state of a freshly-added variable, since Vercel doesn't check all three automatically.

An environment variable in Vercel is scoped to Production, Preview and Development independently — a variable added without checking all three boxes it actually needs is not a global default, it's silently absent everywhere it wasn't checked.

contentSections.title: The same key everywhere is its own risk

contentSections.body: Having fixed the crash by checking the Preview box too, a teammate now has briefdesk's real, live Anthropic key active on every preview deployment anyone opens a PR against — which means every test run, every reviewer poking at a branch, and every stray bot that discovers a preview URL is spending real production API credits.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk has: (1) ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, used to generate real briefs — costs money per call; (2) a Stripe secret key, used to process real payments; (3) a public analytics write key, used to log page views; (4) a database connection string pointing at the production database.
contentSections.question: Which of these should use a separate, non-production credential (a test key, a staging database) for Preview and Development, rather than reusing the same production value? Select all that apply.

items.label: The Anthropic API key — reusing production spends real money on every preview build and PR review, with no cap tied to the actual feature being tested
The Stripe secret key — reusing the live key on preview risks processing real charges against real cards while testing a checkout flow
The analytics write key — low-stakes to share across environments, though a separate key keeps preview/test traffic out of production analytics
The production database connection string — a bug in a preview build could read, write, or delete real user data if pointed at the real database

explanation.anthropic-key: Every preview deployment, every PR, every reviewer clicking around is a real, metered API call against production credits if the key is shared. Stripe's own test-mode keys and Anthropic's separate API keys exist specifically so non-production environments can be exercised without touching the account that actually gets billed for real usage.
explanation.stripe-key: This is the highest-stakes case — a live Stripe key in a preview environment means a developer testing checkout, or an automated test suite running against it, could process an actual charge against an actual card. Stripe's test mode keys exist precisely to make this safe.
explanation.analytics-key: This is the one case where sharing is defensible — a page view logged from a preview deployment isn't dangerous or expensive the way a real AI call or a real charge is. It's still cleaner to use a separate analytics property for non-production traffic so it doesn't pollute real usage numbers, but the cost of not doing so is data-quality, not money or safety.
explanation.database-string: A preview deployment testing an in-progress feature — including one with bugs, by definition, since it hasn't shipped yet — reading or writing against the real production database is a direct path to corrupting real user data. This is the case where sharing the credential is a genuine safety incident waiting to happen, not just a cost concern.

contentSections.synthesis: The deciding question for each secret: **does using it in a non-production environment cost real money, risk real data, or risk real side effects a test run shouldn't have?** If yes — API keys with metered usage, payment credentials, production database access — that environment needs its own separate, low-stakes credential. If the answer is genuinely no, sharing is a minor convenience, not a hazard.

contentSections.body:
In practice, this means most real apps end up with environment-specific variables, not one shared set:

```
# Production — real credentials, real money, real data
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-live-...
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod-host/briefdesk

# Preview + Development — separate, capped or test-mode credentials
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-...          # a key with a lower spend cap, if the provider offers one
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_...               # Stripe's own test mode — no real charges possible
DATABASE_URL=postgres://staging-host/briefdesk_dev  # a separate database entirely
```

The underlying principle is the same one from checking rate limits and cost caps in the Claude-integration module: **a non-production environment shouldn't be able to spend real money or touch real data just by existing.** Scoping variables correctly per environment (this section) and using genuinely separate, low-stakes credentials for non-production ones (this section, taken further) are two different fixes for two related problems, and a real app needs both.

A shared production credential in a non-production environment isn't just a scoping mistake — it means every preview build, PR review, and test run is spending real money or touching real data by default, unless that environment has its own separate, low-stakes credential.

title: Preview deployments and catching a bug before it's live
description: Using a PR's preview URL as a real pre-merge check, and diagnosing when preview behaves differently from production for reasons that have nothing to do with the code changing.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a bug that appears only on a preview deployment as an environment difference rather than a code difference
Build a habitual, concrete checklist for what to verify on a preview URL before approving a PR

contentSections.title: A bug that only exists on the preview URL

contentSections.body: A PR adding briefdesk's export-to-PDF feature looks fine in the diff. On the preview URL, clicking "Export" throws a 500. On the reviewer's own local machine, the exact same branch works perfectly.

contentSections.scenario: The PDF export route calls a third-party PDF-rendering service using an API key. Locally, `.env.local` has that key set (the developer added it months ago for a different feature). On Vercel, the key was only ever added with the "Production" box checked — the same scoping gap from this module's second lesson, this time hitting a different variable.
contentSections.question: Why does this bug appear specifically on the preview URL and nowhere else the code has been run?

options.label: The PDF service's API key isn't scoped to Preview in Vercel, so it's undefined there — local dev has it via .env.local, and production has it via the Production checkbox, but preview has neither
The third-party PDF service itself is having an outage
The reviewer's browser is different from whatever's rendering the preview, causing the discrepancy

feedback.env-gap-again: Right. Three environments, three different sources for the same variable: local dev reads `.env.local` (set months ago and forgotten about), production has the Vercel dashboard's Production-scoped value, and preview has neither — nobody ever checked its box, because the key was added for a feature that, at the time, was never tested on a preview URL. Preview isn't broken; it's the one environment that was never given the credential.
feedback.pdf-service-down: An outage would produce the same failure everywhere the service is called from — local dev and production would fail too, not just preview. The fact that it's preview-specific is itself the evidence against a service-side outage.
feedback.browser-difference: The 500 comes from the server-side route handler, before any HTML reaches a browser — it happens regardless of which browser requests it. Browser differences affect rendering and client-side behavior, not a server route's own crash.

contentSections.mechanism: **The same variable can have a different source of truth in each of three environments, and a gap in any one of them produces a bug that only reproduces in exactly that environment.** This is the general shape of the previous lesson's specific example — worth recognizing on sight, because it recurs with every new external service an app integrates, not just the first one.

contentSections.body: A bug that reproduces in exactly one environment and nowhere else is a strong signal to check environment variable scoping before debugging the feature's logic — the code isn't usually where a same-code-different-behavior bug lives.

contentSections.title: What a preview URL is actually for checking

contentSections.body: A reviewer approves a briefdesk PR after reading the diff carefully — the code looks correct. They never opened the preview URL Vercel posted. The feature is, in fact, broken in a way that's invisible in a diff: a button that's unreachable behind an off-screen modal on real content, not the reviewer's imagination of what it would look like.

contentSections.intro: Turn "I read the diff" into an actual pre-merge check using the one thing a diff can't show: the real, running preview deployment.
contentSections.objectName: a preview-check habit worth actually running before approving a PR

fields.prompt: A code diff is excellent at showing what changed. What does it fail to show, that the preview URL can?

options.label: How the feature actually behaves and looks with real data in a real browser — layout, loading states, whether an API call that depends on an env var actually succeeds
How many lines were added or removed
Which commits are included in the PR

feedback.runtime-behavior: Right — a diff shows the *change*, not the *result* of running that change against a real environment with real data. A missing env var, a layout that breaks with a longer-than-expected string, a network call that silently fails: none of these show up by reading code, only by running it.
feedback.line-count: Line count is visible in the diff itself and isn't the thing a preview URL adds — the whole point of checking preview is seeing something the diff can't show at all.
feedback.commit-history: Commit history is also fully visible in the PR view without ever opening the preview URL — again, not the gap preview-checking closes.

fields.prompt: What's the minimum a reviewer should actually do on the preview URL before approving, beyond just confirming it loads without a 500?

options.label: Actually use the specific feature the PR changed — click the new button, submit the new form, trigger the new state — not just load the homepage and call it checked
Confirm the homepage loads; if it does, the deployment is healthy and that's sufficient
Confirm the URL returns a 200 status code via a quick request

feedback.exercise-the-change: Right — a homepage that loads or a 200 status only proves the deployment succeeded, not that the specific thing the PR changed actually works. The check that matters is exercising the exact feature the diff touched, with real interaction, not just confirming the app is up.
feedback.check-homepage-only: This confirms the build didn't crash on startup, which is necessary but nowhere near sufficient — the PDF export bug from the previous section would sail through a homepage-only check and still be broken.
feedback.check-uptime-only: A 200 response tells you the server responded, not that the feature the PR actually changed works correctly. This is an even weaker check than loading the homepage in a browser.

contentSections.synthesis: A preview-check habit worth keeping: **open the preview URL, and do the specific thing the PR changed** — click the new button, submit the new form, trigger the new state — not just confirm the app boots. Pair that with a quick glance at whether anything env-dependent (an API call, a feature flag) behaves as expected, since that's exactly the class of bug a diff can never reveal and the previous section's PDF bug is a real example of.

contentSections.body:
This doesn't need to be elaborate to be effective — most preview checks take under two minutes:

```
Before approving:
1. Open the preview URL Vercel posted on the PR.
2. Do the specific thing this PR changed — not the whole app, just the diff's feature.
3. If the feature calls an external service or reads an env var, confirm it actually succeeds (not just that the page renders).
4. Only then approve — a clean diff and an unexercised preview URL is a review that skipped the part a diff can't show.
```

The cost of skipping this is exactly what happened with the PDF export bug: a mergeable-looking PR that was, in fact, one unchecked box away from breaking in production the moment it shipped.
Reading a diff proves what changed; opening the preview URL and exercising the specific feature is the only step that proves it actually works — a review that skips it isn't a complete review.

title: Rolling back a bad deploy in under a minute
description: Using Vercel's instant rollback to re-point production at a known-good deployment, instead of a slower git-revert-and-rebuild cycle while the site stays broken.

learningObjectives.text: Sequence the steps of an instant rollback and explain why it's near-instant compared to a redeploy
Compare rollback against git-revert-and-redeploy and identify which situations call for each

contentSections.title: The deploy that broke checkout

contentSections.body: A briefdesk deploy meant to fix a typo also, unintentionally, breaks the export-to-PDF button — a dependency bump in the same PR changed a function's signature nobody updated the caller for. It's live. Real users are hitting it right now.

contentSections.code:
# the instinctive first move
$ git revert HEAD
$ git push origin main
# ...wait for Vercel to detect the push, spin up a build container,
# run `next build` again, upload the new output, repoint the domain...
# (typically 60-180 seconds for a Next.js app, depending on size)
contentSections.question: This does fix the bug, eventually. What's the actual cost of this being the first move, specifically?

options.label: The site stays broken for the entire rebuild — a full build-and-deploy cycle, not an instant fix — even though a known-good version already exists and is sitting right there in Vercel's deployment history
git revert is not a legitimate command to use in this situation at all
Reverting on main is against best practice and should happen on a separate branch first

feedback.broken-during-rebuild: Right. `git revert` + push is correct *eventually*, but it re-runs the entire build pipeline from scratch — a minute or more where checkout is still broken for real users, purely because the fix took the slow path when a faster one existed. The previous, working deployment didn't go anywhere; it's sitting in Vercel's deployment history the whole time, unused.
feedback.not-legitimate: git revert is a perfectly legitimate, correct command here — the problem isn't that it's the wrong tool, it's that it's slower than necessary as the *first* response to a live incident, because it re-triggers a full build before anything improves for users.
feedback.wrong-branch: Whether the revert happens on a branch first or directly on main isn't the actual problem here — either way, the fix still requires a full rebuild before it's live, which is the real source of continued downtime.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The faster fix: Vercel's dashboard → Deployments → find the last known-good deployment → "Promote to Production." This re-points the production domain at a build artifact that already exists and already passed, with no rebuild step at all — typically live again in under a minute, often seconds.

contentSections.body:
The reason this is fast is structural: **every Vercel deployment is an immutable, already-built artifact**, not a mutable server state. Deploying isn't "update the running server" — it's "build a new, complete, independent artifact and point the domain at it." That means the *previous* artifact never stopped existing; it's still fully built, still valid, still one dashboard click away from being live again:

```
Deployments
  ● abc123f  (current, broken)   deployed 4 min ago
  ○ def456a  (previous, known-good)  deployed 2 hours ago   [Promote to Production]
  ○ 789bcde  (older)             deployed yesterday
```

Rollback = pointing the production alias at `def456a` instead of `abc123f`. No build step, no waiting on `next build` to finish, no risk that the emergency fix itself introduces a new bug — it's the exact bytes that were already known to work, five minutes ago.

A rollback re-points the production domain at an already-built, already-working deployment — it's near-instant because nothing rebuilds; a git-revert-and-redeploy is correct but structurally slower, because it re-runs the entire build pipeline first.

contentSections.title: When revert is still the right move

contentSections.body: Rollback fixed checkout in thirty seconds. The buggy PR is still merged into main — the next person to push any unrelated change will rebuild from that same broken commit and undo the rollback without meaning to.

contentSections.scenario: A bad deploy is rolled back at 2:14pm — production is back on the known-good build within a minute. At 2:14pm, the buggy commit is still sitting at the tip of the main branch, unrevered, in git history.
contentSections.question: Is the incident actually resolved at this point, or is there a second step still needed?

options.label: A second step is needed: revert or fix the bug in git too, so the next deploy (from anyone, for any reason) doesn't rebuild from the same broken commit and silently undo the rollback
Fully resolved — the rollback fixed what users see, and that's the actual goal
The rollback was the wrong move to begin with; reverting in git should have been the only step taken

feedback.still-needs-revert: Right. Rollback fixes what's *live* immediately — it does nothing to fix what's in *git*. The broken commit is still the tip of main, and the very next deploy, triggered by any unrelated change, rebuilds from that same broken state and undoes the rollback without anyone intending it to. The incident isn't actually closed until the fix (or a revert) lands in git too.
feedback.fully-resolved: This misses that git and the live deployment are now out of sync — main still points at the broken commit, and any future deploy from main immediately re-introduces the exact bug that was just fixed. The visible symptom is gone; the root cause is still sitting at the tip of the branch.
feedback.should-have-reverted-instead: Both steps were needed, not one instead of the other — rollback correctly bought immediate relief for real users while a proper revert or fix was prepared, which is exactly the sequencing an incident calls for: stop the bleeding first, fix the underlying cause second.

contentSections.concept: **Rollback and git revert solve two different problems on two different timescales — rollback fixes what's live, right now; revert (or a proper fix) keeps the next deploy from undoing that fix.** A real incident response uses rollback for speed and still needs a git-level fix before the story is actually over.

contentSections.body:
The full sequence for a real incident, in order:

1. **Roll back immediately** — "Promote to Production" on the last known-good deployment. This is the emergency brake; it buys time without requiring anyone to think clearly under pressure yet.
2. **Revert or fix the bug in git**, on its own PR, reviewed normally (or fast-tracked if truly urgent) — so main no longer points at the broken commit.
3. **Let that fix deploy normally.** Production is now caught up with git again, on a version that's both live-correct and git-correct.

Skipping step 2 is the trap: rollback feels like the incident is over, because production looks fine again. It's only actually over once git and production agree — otherwise the next unrelated deploy is a landmine nobody's watching for.

Rollback and a git-level fix are both required, in that order — rollback buys immediate relief, but until the broken commit is actually reverted or fixed in git, the very next deploy re-introduces it.

title: Custom domains and what actually breaks when you add one
description: Pointing a purchased domain at a Vercel deployment via DNS records, and auditing what else in the app still refers to the old *.vercel.app URL once the real domain is live.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which DNS record type is needed for an apex domain versus a subdomain pointing at Vercel
Audit an app for hardcoded references to its old deployment URL that break once a custom domain replaces it

contentSections.title: Buying the domain is the easy part

contentSections.body: briefdesk.app costs $18/year from a registrar. Buying it takes two minutes. Making `briefdesk.app` actually load the same app that `briefdesk-abc123.vercel.app` has been serving takes a DNS change that can take anywhere from a few minutes to, in rare cases, up to 48 hours to fully propagate — and until it does, some visitors see the new site and some still see nothing or an error, depending on which DNS server answered their request.

contentSections.scenario: Vercel's domain settings ask for one of two DNS record types depending on whether the domain being added is an apex domain (briefdesk.app itself) or a subdomain (app.briefdesk.app): an A record pointing at Vercel's IP address, or a CNAME record pointing at a Vercel-provided hostname.
contentSections.question: Why can't an apex domain (briefdesk.app, with nothing before the dot) typically use a CNAME the way a subdomain can?

options.label: DNS rules generally don't allow a CNAME record to coexist with the other records (like MX, for email) an apex domain needs — so apex domains use an A record instead, subdomains use CNAME
CNAME records are technically slower to resolve than A records, so apex domains avoid them for performance
There's no real technical difference — either record type works equally well for either kind of domain

feedback.cname-apex-conflict: Right. A CNAME record at the apex (the bare domain, no subdomain) generally can't coexist with other DNS records the domain needs — most notably MX records for email. A subdomain like `app.briefdesk.app` doesn't have that conflict, so it can point at Vercel with a CNAME; the apex domain itself uses an A record pointing at Vercel's IP address instead.
feedback.cname-slower: Resolution speed isn't the reason for the distinction — both record types resolve quickly. The actual constraint is a structural DNS rule about what can coexist at the apex, not a performance difference.
feedback.no-real-difference: There is a real, load-bearing difference — using the wrong record type for an apex domain (a CNAME where an A record is required) can genuinely fail to resolve or break other DNS records like MX. This isn't a preference, it's a protocol-level constraint.

contentSections.concept: **An apex domain and a subdomain have different DNS requirements when pointing at Vercel — A record for the apex, CNAME for a subdomain — because of a structural DNS rule about what can coexist at the root of a domain, not an arbitrary platform choice.** Vercel's domain settings screen tells you which one to add for the specific domain being configured.

contentSections.body:
The practical setup, once the domain is purchased from a registrar (Porkbun, Namecheap, and similar all work the same way here):

```
# In the registrar's DNS settings, for briefdesk.app:
Type   Name   Value
A      @      76.76.21.21        # Vercel's apex IP (shown in Vercel's dashboard for this project)
CNAME  www    cname.vercel-dns.com.
```

Vercel's own project settings show the exact values to use for the specific domain being added — copy those rather than guessing. SSL is handled automatically once DNS resolves correctly; there's no separate certificate step to configure. **What this costs:** the domain itself, roughly $10-20/year depending on the TLD and registrar (`.app` domains run slightly higher than `.com`); Vercel doesn't charge extra to attach a custom domain on the Hobby tier. Propagation delay is the real cost in time, not money — DNS changes are cached across the internet's many resolvers, so different visitors briefly see different states depending on which cached answer their ISP happens to be serving.

An apex domain needs an A record (structural DNS rule); a subdomain can use a CNAME; Vercel's dashboard shows the exact values for the domain being configured — and propagation, not money, is the real delay to plan around.

contentSections.title: The old URL doesn't disappear — it's still hardcoded somewhere

contentSections.body: briefdesk.app is live and working. Two days later, someone tries "Sign in with Google" and it fails — the OAuth redirect URI registered with Google still points at `briefdesk-abc123.vercel.app`, which nobody updated, because adding a custom domain doesn't retroactively fix references to the old one sitting in other systems.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk switches its primary domain from briefdesk-abc123.vercel.app to briefdesk.app. Places the old URL might still be referenced: (1) the OAuth redirect URI registered in Google's developer console, (2) a CORS allowed-origins list in the API server's config, (3) Vercel's own routing, which still resolves the old *.vercel.app URL to the same deployment, (4) hardcoded absolute URLs in email templates linking back to the app.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually break or need updating once the custom domain becomes the primary one? Select all that apply.

items.label: The OAuth redirect URI — Google will reject the auth flow if the redirect URI it receives doesn't exactly match what's registered
The CORS allowed-origins list — requests from the new domain will be blocked by the browser if the API server's CORS config only allows the old origin
Vercel's own routing to the old *.vercel.app URL — this keeps working by default and doesn't need any change
Hardcoded absolute URLs in transactional emails — links in already-sent or newly-sent emails still point at the old domain until the template is updated

explanation.oauth-redirect: OAuth providers match redirect URIs exactly — a briefdesk.app callback won't be accepted if only the old vercel.app URL is registered, and this fails specifically for real users trying to sign in, not for any obviously-related reason at first glance.
explanation.cors-origins: A CORS allowlist that still only names the old origin will cause the browser to block API requests made from pages served at the new domain — a silent, confusing failure that looks like a network problem rather than a configuration one.
explanation.vercel-routing: This one keeps working without any changes — Vercel doesn't stop serving the auto-generated *.vercel.app URL when a custom domain is added; both continue to resolve to the same deployment unless deliberately redirected.
explanation.email-templates: Any template with a hardcoded `https://briefdesk-abc123.vercel.app/...` link keeps generating links to the old URL until the template itself is updated — the custom domain going live doesn't retroactively touch strings baked into unrelated code.

contentSections.synthesis: Adding a custom domain changes what Vercel serves at that domain — it does not automatically update every other system that has the old URL written down somewhere. The audit worth doing before calling a custom-domain migration finished: search the codebase and any connected third-party dashboards (OAuth providers, CORS configs, webhook URLs, email templates) for the old hostname specifically, because none of them get updated by DNS changing.

contentSections.body:
A practical pre-launch checklist for a domain switch:

```
[ ] grep the codebase for the old *.vercel.app hostname — check email templates,
    webhook callback URLs, hardcoded absolute links
[ ] Update OAuth redirect URIs in every connected provider's console
    (Google, GitHub, etc.) to include the new domain
[ ] Update CORS allowed-origins in the API server's config
[ ] Update any webhook subscriptions (Stripe, etc.) pointing at the old domain
[ ] Decide whether to keep the old *.vercel.app URL working (harmless by default)
    or redirect it to the new domain for consistency
```

None of this is exotic — it's the same category of problem as the environment-variable scoping earlier in this module: a value (a URL, in this case) that lives in more than one place, changed in one of them, and quietly stayed stale everywhere else.

A custom domain going live changes what Vercel serves — it does nothing to update the old URL wherever else it's hardcoded (OAuth providers, CORS configs, email templates), and those need their own explicit audit and update.

title: Diagnose seven deployment misconfigurations
description: Seven drills applying the module's filters — deploy pipeline, environment scoping, preview checks, rollback, custom domains — to unfamiliar deployment setups.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's deployment and environment filters to unfamiliar setups at speed
Identify the specific misconfiguration behind a deployment symptom, not just that something is broken

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Set up production and preview environments properly
description: Deploy a real app to Vercel, scope its environment variables correctly across Production/Preview/Development, and prove a rollback actually works before calling the setup done.

learningObjectives.text: Deploy a real app to Vercel with correctly-scoped environment variables across all three environments
Execute and verify a real rollback on a live deployment

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter in this module — the deploy pipeline, environment scoping, preview checks, instant rollback, domain migration hygiene — is easiest to trust once you've actually broken and fixed a live deployment yourself, on purpose, rather than reading about someone else doing it. This lab deploys a real app (briefdesk-shaped or otherwise) with properly separated environments, and proves the rollback path actually works before calling it done.

contentSections.title: Deploy it for real, then break it on purpose
contentSections.brief: Take a real app you have — even a small one — and deploy it to Vercel with production and preview genuinely separated: different credentials where it matters, a verified preview-check habit, and a rollback you've actually tested rather than assumed would work. The point isn't a perfect app; it's a deployment setup you could trust during a real incident.
contentSections.deliverable: A live app with separate environments and a tested rollback

stages.title: Deploy and scope environment variables
stages.instructions: Connect a real repo to Vercel and get it live. For every environment variable the app needs, decide deliberately: does Preview need this too, and does Preview need a separate, non-production value (a test API key, a staging database) rather than the production one? Configure each variable's scoping explicitly rather than accepting whatever the first checkbox happened to be.
stages.checkpoint: The app is live on a production URL, and every environment variable has a documented, deliberate scoping decision — not a default nobody looked at.

stages.title: Open a PR and actually check its preview
stages.instructions: Make a small, real change on a branch and open a PR. On the resulting preview URL, exercise the specific thing that changed — don't just confirm the homepage loads. If the app has anything env-dependent, confirm it actually works on preview, not just that the page renders.
stages.checkpoint: A PR exists with a preview URL that was actually exercised, and you can say specifically what you checked and what you'd have missed by only reading the diff.

stages.title: Break it and roll it back
stages.instructions: Merge a deliberately small, obviously bad change to production (a typo in a visible label is enough — nothing destructive). Once it's live and broken, use Vercel's dashboard to promote the previous deployment back to production. Time how long the rollback actually takes from click to live. Then fix the bug properly in git so the next deploy doesn't undo the rollback.
stages.checkpoint: A real rollback has been executed and timed, and the underlying bug has been fixed in git — not just papered over by the rollback.

rubric.criterion: The app is genuinely live with a working deploy pipeline
rubric.meets: A real push to the production branch results in a real, working update at a real URL, without manual intervention.

rubric.criterion: Environment variables are deliberately scoped, not defaulted
rubric.meets: Each variable's Production/Preview/Development scoping was a decision, documented in one sentence each — and anything cost- or data-sensitive uses a separate non-production value.

rubric.criterion: A preview URL was actually exercised, not just loaded
rubric.meets: The specific feature a PR changed was clicked through and verified on the live preview deployment, with a stated example of what that check would have caught that a diff review alone would have missed.

rubric.criterion: A rollback was actually executed and timed
rubric.meets: A real rollback happened on a real (harmless) broken deploy, with an honest recorded time from decision to live-again — not a description of how rollback would theoretically work.

rubric.criterion: The underlying bug was fixed in git after the rollback
rubric.meets: Production and git agree again by the end of the lab — the broken commit isn't still sitting at the tip of the branch waiting to be reintroduced by the next deploy.

contentSections.body: The real test of a deployment setup isn't whether it looks correct in the dashboard — it's whether you've actually broken it and gotten back to a working state, on purpose, before it happens for real and unplanned.

title: Checkpoint — Deploying and Managing Environments
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User, two from Integrating the Claude API Properly. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Deploying and Managing Environments

questions.from: This module — Deploying and Managing Environments
questions.prompt: A variable is added in Vercel's dashboard with only the 'Production' box checked. What happens when a Preview build reads it?

options.label: It's undefined in Preview — scoping is exclusive per environment, with no automatic fallback from Production
Preview automatically inherits the Production value
The build fails to compile entirely

questions.explanation: Each environment's scoping is independent — a variable not checked for Preview simply doesn't exist there, with no automatic inheritance.

questions.from: This module — Deploying and Managing Environments
questions.prompt: Why does promoting a previous Vercel deployment to production (rollback) fix a bad deploy faster than git revert + push?

options.label: The previous deployment is already a fully built artifact — promoting it is a routing change with no rebuild, while revert-and-push re-triggers the full build pipeline
Rollback uses a faster build system than a normal deploy
There's no real speed difference between the two

questions.explanation: Deployments are immutable built artifacts — rollback just changes which one the domain points to, with no build step at all.

questions.from: This module — Deploying and Managing Environments
questions.prompt: After a successful rollback, what step is still required before the incident is actually resolved?

options.label: Revert or fix the bug in git, so the next unrelated deploy doesn't rebuild from the same broken commit
Nothing further — the live site looking correct again means the incident is closed
Manually disable all future deploys until further notice

questions.explanation: Rollback fixes what's live; it doesn't touch git. The broken commit is still at the tip of the branch until it's explicitly reverted or fixed.

questions.from: This module — Deploying and Managing Environments
questions.prompt: Adding a custom domain and confirming the homepage loads correctly — is the domain migration finished at that point?

options.label: Not necessarily — third-party systems (OAuth redirect URIs, CORS configs, webhook URLs) that hardcode the old domain need their own separate audit and update
Yes — a working homepage on the new domain confirms the whole migration is complete
Only if the old *.vercel.app URL is deliberately disabled afterward

questions.explanation: Nothing about DNS changing updates a URL hardcoded in an external system's own dashboard — those need an explicit, separate check.

questions.from: Previous module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A form has three identically-styled solid-blue buttons. What's the actual problem, and the fix?

options.label: Nothing is visually dominant, so the eye has no signal for the primary action — keep one solid, demote the others to outline or text
All three should be a different color entirely
Nothing is wrong — consistent button styling is good practice

questions.explanation: Equal weight across every element means no signal for which one matters most — hierarchy needs deliberate contrast between elements.

questions.from: Previous module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A list renders items.map() off a useState that starts as []. What does the screen show before the fetch resolves, and why?

options.label: Nothing — an empty array and a genuinely-empty loaded result render identically, since there's no separate loading state
A default loading spinner appears automatically
A runtime error, since items starts empty

questions.explanation: Both states render as nothing without an explicit status value distinguishing 'still loading' from 'loaded, and empty.'

questions.from: Previous module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A grid uses grid-cols-3 with no responsive prefixes. What's the mobile-first fix?

options.label: grid-cols-1 as the unprefixed default, with md:/lg: prefixes adding columns at wider breakpoints
grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-1, reducing columns only at large widths
No fix needed — Tailwind automatically adjusts column count for narrow screens

questions.explanation: Mobile-first means writing the narrowest layout unprefixed and adding wider-screen overrides — unprefixed classes apply everywhere by default with no automatic adjustment.

questions.from: Previous module — Styling and UX That Doesn't Fight the User
questions.prompt: A five-step signup flow gets a full visual redesign and completion rate doesn't move, with drop-off spread evenly across all five steps. What does this suggest?

options.label: The friction is likely the step count itself, not any individual screen's visual quality — reducing steps is the next thing worth trying
The redesign should be attempted again, more carefully
Nothing can be done — some users simply won't complete signup

questions.explanation: Even drop-off unmoved by visual polish points at the number of steps as the friction, not the quality of any one screen.

questions.from: Older module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: Why can an Anthropic API key never be sent to the browser, even over HTTPS?

options.label: Anything shipped to client-side JavaScript is readable via dev tools regardless of transport encryption — HTTPS protects data in transit, not code visibility at the destination
HTTPS doesn't encrypt requests originating from browsers
It's fine as long as the key isn't hardcoded as a plain string

questions.explanation: HTTPS secures the connection, not the visibility of code and values once they're shipped to and running in the browser.

questions.from: Older module — Integrating the Claude API Properly
questions.prompt: What's the actual benefit of streaming a Claude response into the UI token by token?

options.label: Perceived latency drops — the user sees progress within a second or two instead of a blank wait for the full response, even though total completion time is unchanged
The model generates the response faster when streaming is enabled
It reduces the total token cost of the request

questions.explanation: Streaming changes what the user perceives during generation, not the model's actual generation speed or the request's cost.
